title: No cure, no vaccine: Experts warn of rare Bourbon virus after first NY case
summary: A Long Island patient was hospitalized after researchers confirmed the first Bourbon virus case in New York transmitted by the common lone star tick.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the alarming rise of Powassan virus, a rare tick-borne disease, with 15 cases reported this year, following a record 76 in 2025.

A rarely diagnosed tick-borne virus with no vaccine or specific treatment has been confirmed in New York for the first time, prompting researchers to warn that additional infections may be going undiagnosed.

The Bourbon virus, "transmitted through the common lone star tick, could soon begin to complicate diagnoses if it becomes more prevalent this summer and in coming years," Stony Brook Medicine warned in a news release reporting on a study of the virus.
Only six human cases have been reported since Bourbon virus was first identified in Bourbon County, Kansas, where the first known patient was diagnosed in 2014. That patient later died.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
The virus has been linked to at least two deaths, including the original 2014 case and another reported in 2026. Researchers believe, however, that additional infections have likely gone undiagnosed.
Symptoms of Bourbon virus include fever, fatigue, rash, headache, body aches and nausea. Because there is no commercially available diagnostic test, doctors have a difficult time identifying it.
Adult female lone star ticks are identifiable by a white dot, or lone star, on their backs. (iStock)
Many healthcare providers are also unfamiliar with the virus, "thus increasing the possibility of misdiagnosis," the release said.

A team of researchers led by Stony Brook Medicine confirmed the first case of Bourbon virus in New York in a patient from Long Island who developed severe symptoms and an eight-fold rise in antibody titers of the Bourbon virus. The patient was hospitalized.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There are a lot of lone star ticks in New York and in the Northeast, we have dense populations and when someone is infected with Bourbon virus symptoms they are similar to other tick-borne infections," Luis Marcos, Stony Brook Medicine professor and director of the Tick-borne Disease Clinic, said in the news release.
"For these reasons, the Bourbon virus is likely more prevalent than we think in our region, and other cases are likely not being diagnosed."
Marcos and his co-authors said their findings show the need for expanded surveillance and better testing to improve diagnosis and track the spread of Bourbon virus.
People bitten by ticks should remove them as soon as possible. (iStock)

"Without identifying the cause of an infection, the chances of developing accurate diagnostic tests or effective treatments are minimal," he said. "That is why it is so important to first understand the true impact of the virus in high-risk areas."
According to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC), "The lone star tick is widely distributed in the Northeast, South and Midwest United States."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The tiny, blood-feeding, parasitic arachnid has established populations in Arkansas, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and West Virginia, according to the CDC.
Lone star ticks are an "aggressive tick," according to the agency.
To avoid tick bites, experts advise wearing long pants and sleeves, using insect repellent and avoiding overgrown areas. (iStock)
"The adult female is distinguished by a white dot or ‘lone star’ on her back. The nymph and adult females most frequently bite humans and spread disease," the CDC reports.
Despite the Bourbon virus’ severity, "only a select few [ticks] bite and transmit bacteria, viruses and parasites (pathogens) that cause diseases in people," according to the CDC.
To avoid tick bites, people should wear protective clothing, such as pants they can tuck into boots and long-sleeve shirts.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Experts also recommend applying insect repellent, such as permethrin, to clothing and outdoor gear, not directly on the skin.
Stay out of tall grass and on well-beaten trails whenever possible because ticks thrive in overgrown and heavily wooded areas.

Check for ticks after spending time outdoors and remove them as soon as you find them. Seek medical attention if you develop fever, rash, fatigue or other flu-like symptoms in the days or weeks following a tick bite.
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Skin condition under the eyes goes viral, and doctors warn it could signal hidden health issue
summary: Doctors reveal how low ferritin levels in the body can cause dark under-eye circles, pale skin and fatigue even as they warn against self-treating an iron deficiency.
story: Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name ‘ferritin face.’
Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name "ferritin face."
Experts say there's some truth behind the trend with important caveats.

Ferritin can be thought of as the body's "iron storage vault," according to Dr. Josef Hadeed, a double board-certified plastic surgeon at Hadeed Plastic Surgery in Beverly Hills, California. It is a protein that stores iron inside the body's cells and releases it when needed.
LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW
"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," Hadeed told Fox News Digital.
Low iron levels can compromise skin elasticity, which can make the tissue appear thinner and less resilient, the doctor said.
Dark under-eye circles can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media with the name "ferritin face." (iStock)
When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable, Hadeed noted.
Symptoms of low ferritin
Besides pale skin and dark under-eye circles, other symptoms may signal that someone is lacking iron.
CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS

"The severity of these symptoms generally increases as ferritin decreases," Dane Thomas, a Texas-based hematology/oncology physician associate who specializes in the care of patients with hematologic disorders and cancer, told Fox News Digital.
Low energy, fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, headaches, fainting, brittle or thin nails, hair loss, cravings to chew ice and restless legs syndrome are a few signs, according to Thomas.

"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," an expert told Fox News Digital. (iStock)
"Some patients also experience decreased exercise tolerance, difficulty concentrating or shortness of breath with exertion," he said.
Other symptoms can include pounding or "whooshing" in the ears, a sore or smooth tongue, rapid heartbeat, intolerance to cold and poor sleep, according to the American Society of Hematology.
Underlying conditions

Beyond cosmetic concerns, ferritin face may signal an underlying medical condition, including chronic bleeding, gastrointestinal disorders or cancers or malabsorption, according to hematological experts.

With the rise in bariatric surgery, more patients are developing iron deficiency due to impaired iron absorption, Thomas said. Certain over-the-counter acid-suppressing medications, including proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and H2-receptor blockers, may also contribute to low iron.
"This is not something that someone should self-treat."
While treating iron deficiency is important, identifying and addressing its underlying cause is equally critical, he said.

"Whenever possible, I work with my patients to determine why their iron deficiency developed so we can reduce the likelihood that it will recur," Thomas told Fox News Digital. "This often involves collaboration with gastroenterologists, gynecologists or other specialists to evaluate for sources of blood loss or malabsorption."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Pregnancy, heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent blood donation can also contribute to lower iron levels. Vegetarians, vegans and those who follow diets that do not include iron-rich foods may also be at risk, according to the American Society of Hematologists.
Diagnosis and treatment
If a person thinks they may have low ferritin, it is important to see a physician.

"This is not something that someone should self-treat, and I always advise them to seek professional help," Hadeed advised. "Unlike water-soluble vitamins, the body has no easy mechanism to excrete excess iron, and over-supplementation can lead to increased levels of iron in the body, which can affect the liver and heart."
When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable. (iStock)

A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. Further evaluation may include stool and urine tests to look for blood, along with endoscopy to examine the esophagus, stomach and colon. Women may also undergo a gynecological evaluation, according to experts.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Treatment for iron deficiency may include oral supplementation and, in cases of severe anemia, intravenous (IV) iron or blood transfusions.
"The biggest drawback of oral iron is gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort and stomach upset," Thomas noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"These side effects can often be minimized by taking iron every other day rather than daily, a strategy that also maintains excellent absorption for many patients."
He also recommends spacing them apart from calcium supplements, dairy products and antacids, which can affect absorption.
A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. (iStock)
Following a diet that includes iron-rich foods can also help, according to the American Society of Hematology website.

Some examples include beef, pork, or lamb; organ meats like liver, chicken, turkey, duck and fish (especially shellfish, sardines and anchovies); leafy greens, such as broccoli, kale, turnip greens and collard greens; legumes, including lima beans, peas, pinto beans and black-eyed peas; and iron-enriched pastas, grains, rice and cereals.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ferritin face is reversible, Hadeed emphasized.
Once iron stores are safely restored and hemoglobin levels rebound, the skin recovers its healthy capillary flush, and dark under-eye circles tend to fade over several months.
Amy McGorry is a contributing health writer for Fox News Digital. Follow her on Twitter @amymcgorry.

title: American Red Cross declares national blood crisis as type O supply drops to dangerous levels
summary: The American Red Cross declared a blood crisis across the nation as donations hit a four-year summer low, forcing limits on type O blood distributions to hospitals.
story: The American Red Cross declares a critical national blood shortage crisis as supply levels hit dangerously low levels across the United States. Dr. Baia Lasky, medical director for the organization, joins 'Fox & Friends First' to explain the severe impact on hospitals, detail the urgent need for type O donations, and guide viewers on how to help.
The American Red Cross has declared a "blood crisis" across the nation.
The organization released a warning about the second-ever blood supply crisis this week after blood donations fell to a four-year summer low.
This decline worsens an emergency shortage that "threatens the availability of lifesaving blood for patients across the country," the organization wrote in a press release.
MICROPLASTICS DETECTED IN MOST HEART ATTACK PATIENTS' BLOOD IN STARTLING NEW STUDY

The Red Cross is now limiting distributions of type O blood to hospitals, as the nation’s largest single provider of blood products now has less than a one-day national supply of type O positive blood.
Type O blood accounts for about 60% of Red Cross blood distributions and is essential for both everyday patient care and medical emergencies.
A volunteer is pictured donating blood during an American Red Cross blood drive at Hollywood's Magic Castle in Los Angeles, California, July 28, 2026. (Getty Images)
Type O positive is the most commonly transfused blood type, according to the Red Cross, and can be safely given to about 80% of patients.
Type O negative remains the universal blood type "relied upon when every second counts."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
While thousands of Americans show up to donate blood, these donations are reportedly not keeping up with hospital demand during summer trauma season.

This summer’s conditions, amid extreme heat, poor air quality and foodborne illnesses, have contributed to lower donor turnout, the Red Cross reported. Other blood collectors have also reported critical shortages this summer.
A clinician deposits a blood collection tube during an American Red Cross blood drive at Hollywood's Magic Castle on July 28, 2026, in Los Angeles.  (Getty Images)
The Red Cross advised that just three more donors at each blood drive can end the crisis and stabilize the blood supply.
It encourages Americans to book an appointment by using the Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or by calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767).
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Biomedical Services, shared information about the developing emergency in a statement.

"The Red Cross takes its responsibility as the nation’s largest single provider of blood products incredibly seriously and has worked tirelessly to strengthen the blood supply for our hospital partners," he said.
Pedestrians walk past the American Red Cross Blood Donation Center in Boston, Massachusetts, on July 14, 2026. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)
Following the organization’s first national blood crisis in January 2022, Hrouda said the Red Cross has put "additional safeguards" in place to help "prevent a crisis like that from happening again."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"But this summer, blood donations simply are not keeping pace with hospital demand, and inventories — especially type O blood — remain under significant strain," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Every donation has the potential to help save lives, and we urgently need everyone who is eligible to make an appointment to give blood as soon as possible."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Shark Week warnings as experts reveal 6 ways to reduce your risk of a shark bite
summary: White shark activity is ramping up along both coasts this August, and experts share six critical tips to avoid a dangerous shark encounter.
story: A great white shark's powerful breach near a boogie boarder off Newport Beach early Saturday created a heart-pounding scene as onlookers watched the massive animal explode from the water nearby.
Shark sightings are common each summer from coast to coast — and though attacks are rare, they do happen.
In August, shark activity begins to ramp up as they migrate and feed along the way, often bringing different species close to shore, according to experts.

Dr. Chris Lowe, professor of marine biology and director of the Shark Lab at California State University, Long Beach (CSULB), confirmed there has been an increase in white shark activity so far this year.
SHARK SIGHTINGS SPIKE NEAR AMERICA'S BEACHES AS JULY 4 CROWDS HEAD TO SHORE FOR WEEKEND
"We expect by August, September or October to see even more sharks off the Southern California coast," he told Fox News Digital.
Even in waters where sharks are frequently found, human encounters rarely lead to bites, experts say. (iStock)

Wyatt Wernath, national spokesperson for the American Lifeguard Association and a retired ocean rescue chief based in Cocoa Beach, Florida, said they've seen typical numbers for this time of year, although there have been "a couple little nibbles" where people were "bit on the heels or the toes."
For those swimming or surfing in the ocean, the experts shared the following six tips to avoid a dangerous shark encounter.
No. 1: Know before you go
Before visiting a new beach, experts advise locating lifeguards and checking for shark sightings, rip currents, jellyfish and other hazards.
10-FOOT GREAT WHITE SHARK SPOTTED SWIMMING DANGEROUSLY CLOSE TO YOUNG PEOPLE

It's important to recognize and understand the flag systems on the beach that can signal certain conditions, Wernath noted. Red flags typically indicate high hazard, yellow flags mean heed caution and green flags mean low hazard.
Red flags typically indicate high hazard, yellow flags mean heed caution and green flags mean low hazard. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
A purple or blue flag indicates the presence of marine life. Combination red and blue flags signal hazardous marine life, such as a shark or dangerous jellyfish.
"If you can prepare yourself by knowing before you go, you’re going to have a much safer and enjoyable vacation or trip to the open water where the sharks live," Wernath said.
No. 2: Avoid other animal activity
Other suspicious animal activity in the water — such as fish, birds and even seals — could mean a shark is nearby.
"If you see the water percolating on the top, that's the fish running from the predators," Wernath said. "Don't go in the water, get out of the water."
SHARK WEEK SHOCKER AS GREAT WHITE BREACHES JUST YARDS FROM OBLIVIOUS BOOGIE BOARDER
"If you see birds diving into the water, and they're feeding kind of erratically, don't go into the water."
Lowe, who runs the California Shark Beach Safety Program, also recommends avoiding dead marine life that could attract sharks.
Other suspicious animal activity in the water — such as fish, birds and even seals — could mean a shark is nearby. (JOSEPH PREZIOSO/AFP via Getty Images)

"If you're out on your surfboard and a seal climbs on your board, that seal isn't trying to bond with you. It's probably trying to get out of the water because it knows there's a big shark around," he said.
SHARK WEEK PUTS SHARK BITE SURVIVAL IN FOCUS WITH ER DOC'S EXPERT TIPS
Avoid bait balls, which are dense schools of fish targeted by predators, Lowe advised. If one forms beneath your surfboard, move away to avoid an approaching shark.
No. 3: Don't stray too far from shore
While some "toe nibblers" in Florida have been known to attack on the shoreline, deep-water predators pose a risk as well, the experts warned.
"They might occasionally bite a person, but we don't really know why."
California has about three shark bites per year and a fatality about every third year, according to Lowe — but numbers change as the population increases and more people seek out offshore recreation.
"When people start going out into the open ocean ... they may be encountering shark species that haven't been around people before," he said. "And therefore, you're a novelty."
Fishing content creator Henry Gibbs was bitten by a grey reef shark while spearfishing in Fiji. (Getty Images)
Ocean spear fishing and kayak fishing are examples of "risky" excursions that have gained popularity in the last few decades, Lowe noted.

"Not only do you have a bloody fish on the end of your spear, but you're out around sharks that might not have been around people before," he said. "So, we just don't know how those sharks will react."
SHARK WEEK FANS MAY WANT TO THINK TWICE BEFORE EATING THIS OCEAN PREDATOR, EXPERTS WARN
"If you're kayak fishing, and you've got your legs in the water, and you’ve got a bloody fish, your leg could get mistaken by an excited shark trying to steal your fish."
When diving or snorkeling, it’s important not to present yourself "as prey," Wernath warned.
No. 4: Skip dawn and dusk swims; never swim alone
Dawn and dusk are peak feeding times for many sharks, increasing the risk of encounters.
Because sharks can mistake people for prey, Lowe recommends avoiding murky water and shiny jewelry that can mimic fish scales.
Because sharks can mistake people for prey, experts recommend avoiding murky water and shiny jewelry that can mimic fish scales. (iStock)
The chances of being bitten are statistically lower when swimming in a group than alone, Lowe said — and if trouble arises, others are there to help.
No. 5: React quickly
During a close encounter, it's important to confirm that the animal is actually a shark, as dolphin and stingray fins can look similar in the water.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Unlike dolphins and stingrays, which typically show a single fin before disappearing underwater, sharks often reveal both their dorsal and tail fins.
"Tail fins will be moving more in a sweeping motion," Wernath said. "It won't go under gradually like a submarine. It won't arc like a dolphin in a rolling fashion."
In an aerial view, a juvenile white shark swims in the clear, shallow water of the Pacific Ocean off the coast of La Jolla on Nov. 22, 2023, in San Diego, California. (Getty Images)
If a shark is identified, give it space and calmly exit the water.

"Don't splash, don't cause a commotion, which will attract the shark, but just get out," Lowe said. "If you're on a surfboard or a boogie board, try to pull yourself up onto it, and just don't present yourself as prey."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If you see the shark, always keep your eyes on it," he advised. "Follow it, track it, let the shark know you see it, turn your body toward it."
"If the shark comes closer, you can just slowly back up and keep watching it. If you lose track of it, the first place you should always look is behind you."
Unlike dolphins and stingrays, which typically show a single fin before disappearing underwater, sharks often reveal both their dorsal and tail fins. (iStock)
A shark approaching from behind is usually trying to investigate without being noticed. Once it realizes it has been spotted, however, "most of the time, the gig is up," Lowe said.
If it continues to approach, he recommends giving it "a good bop in the nose" to discourage it from coming closer.
"If the shark gets really close, I'm always an advocate of striking out at them. I think humans need to let sharks know that they're not supposed to get close to us," he added.
No. 6: Respect the species
Experts say the key to safely coexisting with sharks is respecting their habitat and behavior while avoiding actions that could make people appear to be prey.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"They're much more intelligent than we give them credit for," Wernath said, noting that they carefully assess potential prey before attacking. "They’re hunters. They're going to look around and make sure they can get to a prey without getting hurt."
The biggest misconception about sharks is that if they’re nearby, they’re going to bite you, Lowe said, adding that research proves this "simply isn't true."
CSULB Shark Lab researcher Dr. Ryan Logan spear tags a great white shark off Huntington Beach, California, on Sunday, March 9, 2025. (Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Although human and shark populations have grown thanks to conservation efforts, shark bites haven't increased as expected.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"They might occasionally bite a person, but we don't really know why," Lowe went on. "We don't know if they're biting because they mistake us as food ... [or] because they feel we're a threat."

"Based on our last six years of data using drones, we see white sharks around people pretty much every day, and they seem to largely ignore people," he added. "What that clearly tells me is that humans are not on any shark's menu."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Dem senator presses OpenAI, Anthropic for answers in AI hacking probe
summary: Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester demands security logs and transcripts from OpenAI and Anthropic after AI agents allegedly hacked third parties during testing.
story: Former Pentagon A.I. Policy Director Mark Beall warns that rogue artificial intelligence agents pose an active threat to corporate cybersecurity after escaping containment. Beall addresses recent comments from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman regarding the rapid approach of technological singularity. He emphasizes the urgent need for robust regulatory frameworks to prevent unchecked autonomous software from executing sophisticated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure.

Revelations of OpenAI and Anthropic artificial intelligence agents hacking third parties has drawn the "serious concern" of Sen. Lisa Blunt Blunt Rochester, D-Del., who is now seeking answers from the two businesses incorporated as Public Benefit Companies (PBC) in her state.

In separate letters dated Thursday to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, viewed by Fox News Digital, Blunt Rochester has requested detailed timelines, model instructions, internal approvals, security logs and complete transcripts from the companies’ cyber evaluations.
The member of the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee gave both companies until Sept. 6 to respond.
AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS

Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, D-Del., is the ranking member on the Senate's Science, Manufacturing and Competitiveness Subcommittee, which has jurisdiction over oversight of science and technology research, development and policy. (Annabelle Gordon/Reuters)

"These incidents mark the first publicly confirmed instances of a frontier AI model autonomously launching unauthorized attacks on real people and companies, underscoring the urgent need for federal oversight of frontier AI systems," Blunt Rochester wrote to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, calling for federal testing standards, containment rules and disclosure requirements for evaluations of powerful AI systems.

Her concern follows another letter Monday, as first reported by Fox News Digital, from a coalition of 15 red-state attorneys general warning Altman to preserve documents and halt certain high-risk cybersecurity tests after an experimental artificial intelligence agent allegedly escaped a controlled environment and carried out a multi-day hack into outside computer systems.

One day later, the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute (AISI) identified 19 cases in which AI agents took actions outside the authorized scope of testing. Two involved OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, while 17 involved Anthropic’s Mythos 5.
OPENAI'S SAM ALTMAN WANTS TO NEGOTIATE A 5% STAKE IN COMPANY FOR US IF COMPETITORS AGREE TO KEY PROVISION

"Anthropic models’ repeated attacks on third parties with no knowledge of, or role in, Anthropic and AISI’s evaluations demonstrate an alarming pattern of malicious behavior," Rochester's letter to Amodei read. "Furthermore, the successful attempts by these models to gain unauthorized internet access across multiple sandbox testing environments meant to be cut off from the public internet highlight serious issues with Anthropic’s testing partnerships and procedures.
READ THE AISI REPORT – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:
"To be clear, 'misunderstanding[s]' and 'misconfiguration[s]' with sandbox partners are unacceptable when the stakes are this high.
"We cannot wait for a more consequential incident before establishing federal testing standards, containment requirements, and disclosure obligations for frontier model evaluations.
"Left unaddressed, these gaps could allow a future model, potentially one with greater capability or less oversight, to compromise critical infrastructure, financial systems, or sensitive data."

These investigations carry a distinct Delaware dimension: OpenAI and Anthropic are organized as Delaware PBCs — legal structures that allow them to operate for profit but requires their directors to weigh more than shareholder returns.
KARR BLUETOOTH FLAW EXPOSES 2.2M CARS TO THEFT RISK

Under Delaware law, a PBC board must balance three things: its stockholders' financial interests, the interests of people materially affected by the company's conduct and the specific public benefit written into the company's charter.
READ THE LETTER TO OPENAI – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

"This incident marks an important moment for AI safety and we take the questions raised by the Attorneys General seriously," OpenAI wrote in a statement to Fox News Digital after Monday's letter from the state AGs.

"We are conducting a thorough review along with external advisors and with oversight from the Safety and Security Committee of the Board of Directors. Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with the Attorneys General and other relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly."
Rochester wants records related to the AI agent hacking now, too.
CLICKLOCK MAC MALWARE LOCKS APPS UNTIL YOU GIVE IN

"I appreciate that OpenAI has published preliminary findings, is coordinating with third parties on remediation, and is reviewing its approach to model testing," she wrote to Altman, adding to Amodei, "I appreciate Anthropic’s voluntary review of its cybersecurity evaluations and public disclosure of the findings, and I encourage other companies to follow suit.

"However, these incidents demonstrate the potential risks of deploying pre-release models internally, particularly when safeguards are reduced, even when strictly for testing and evaluation," she wrote to both CEOs.
READ THE LETTER TO ANTHROPIC – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

OpenAI disclosed in July that GPT-5.6 Sol and an internal prototype escaped an internal sandbox while their normal cybersecurity restrictions were disabled. The models allegedly accessed Hugging Face's database and other services, launched roughly 17,000 attacks, used stolen credentials and exploited at least one previously unknown vulnerability.

A separate test conducted by contractor Irregular allegedly allowed an OpenAI model onto the public internet because of a configuration error. The model mistook a real website for a target in a simulated hacking challenge and exploited a live security vulnerability.

"AISI identified 19 instances in which an agent took unsanctioned action beyond the scope of the evaluation. Seventeen of the 19 instances involved Anthropic’s Mythos 5; two involved OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol," Rochester wrote.

The institute’s most serious findings included an agent attempting to place malicious code into a widely used open-source project on GitHub, creating fake identities to pressure a human maintainer, contacting real people and leaving public instructions that other AI systems could use to continue the operation. The maintainer rejected the code, and investigators reported finding no resulting real-world harm.
PAIDWORK BREACH EXPOSES 23M USER RECORDS
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman talks to reporters following a meeting with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C., on June 3, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

Blunt Rochester’s Anthropic letter separately cites three incidents in which Claude models allegedly gained unauthorized internet access and attacked three undisclosed organizations during cyber evaluations conducted with standard safeguards disabled.
Two of the Anthropic models reportedly recognized that they had reached the open internet and were interacting with real targets but continued their attacks.
"It is particularly concerning that Anthropic’s first identified security breach dates back to April 2026 and was not identified until three months later," Blunt Rochester wrote to Amodei.

"This is precisely the kind of emergent, autonomous behavior and offensive cyber capability that Congress, the intelligence community, and experts have repeatedly warned could outpace existing safeguards and could pose a severe threat to the safety and security of all Americans," she added in both letters.
FOX NEWS POLL: MOVE OVER BIG BROTHER, VOTERS SEE BIG TECH AS GREATER THREAT TO US

Anthropic Co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei speaks at the "How AI Will Transform Business in the Next 18 Months" panel during INBOUND 2025 at Moscone Center in San Francisco, Calif., on Sept. 4, 2025. (Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot)

The requested records go beyond basic incident reports. Blunt Rochester is seeking the prompts and full instructions given to the models, time-stamped accounts of how the breaches unfolded, the identities or positions of officials authorized to reduce safety controls and an explanation of why automated monitoring did not immediately detect and stop the activity.
She also asked whether federal agencies were notified, whether the companies are confident they discovered the full extent of the unauthorized access and whether previous incidents went unreported.

Blunt Rochester has a federal oversight basis for pursuing the information. She represents the state whose corporate law governs both companies and is the ranking Democrat on the Senate's Science, Manufacturing and Competitiveness Subcommittee, which has jurisdiction over oversight of science and technology research, development and policy.

Her position does not make her Delaware’s corporate regulator — that role falls principally to state officials and courts — and the companies’ PBC status does not automatically give a U.S. senator access to their internal files.
Blunt Rochester could, however, use the companies’ responses — or a refusal to respond — to press for hearings, legislation or committee-level compulsory action.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Given the significance of this incident, transparency with Congress is essential to ensure that the oversight and safety frameworks governing increasingly autonomous, cyber-capable AI systems keep pace with their capabilities," Blunt Rochester's letters concluded.
Fox News Digital reached out to Altman and Amodei for comment on Blunt Rochester's requests Thursday morning.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Unearthed paper exposes Dem House hopeful's 'insane' proposal for meeting climate goals
summary: Manny Rutinel's resurfaced paper argued governments should incentivize ranchers to transition to plant-based farming in Colorado's top cattle district.
story: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins outlines the USDA's $500 million FIELDS Program aimed at increasing domestic fertilizer production. She stresses that food security is a national security issue, critical for America's self-reliance in feeding and fueling its population for the next 250 years, and discusses advancing farming technology.

Manny Rutinel, Democratic candidate for Congress in Colorado's 8th Congressional District, once co-authored a paper that argued that livestock — not fossil fuels — should be more of a focus to combat global warming.
"Simply put, achieving the Paris Agreement goals will be nearly impossible without ambitious policies that reform our food system," Rutinel wrote in a 2022 paper with the Environmental Law Institute.
"Despite the growing awareness of animal agriculture’s climate impact, climate policy and action have historically focused on electricity and fuel use."
EUROPE'S 'GREEN IDEOLOGY' CLIMATE AGENDA RISKS CRUSHING ITS INDUSTRY, ENVIRONMENT MINISTER WARNS

Rep. Manny Rutinel, the Democratic candidate for the 8th Congressional District, poses for a portrait at the House Chamber of Colorado State Capitol building in Denver, Colorado, on Friday, February 20, 2026. (Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post)

The resurfaced paper is just the most recent resurfaced content complicating the political calculus for Rutinel as he strives to convince voters that his past rhetoric on climate and farming is not fully representative of his views now.
Four years since the publication of his work, Rutinel's election very well could depend on the heavy ranching presence in his district.

Colorado’s 8th district is Colorado’s leading producer of beef cattle and dairy, accounting for 26% of the state’s output, according to Upstate Colorado Economic Development. Of its 2.5 million acres, 75% are devoted to farming and raising livestock.
In recent months, Rutinel has worked to convince voters that he recognizes the industry's importance.

"Like all industry, there are bad apples, and I’ve spoken out against those bad apples that cause extreme and unnecessary animal cruelty in parts of the food industry and against the environmental cost of unsustainable food practices," he said.

"They’re good stewards of the land, they care for their animals, and they are the backbone of our economy and our communities. Colorado ranchers are my friends and neighbors, and I’ve gotten to know them," he added.
BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT FLIP-FLOPS ON CONVERSION THERAPY AFTER LEFT-WING BACKLASH
Cattle look at a rancher who inspects them on a farm from a truck. (Jonne Roriz/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

But through advocacy in college, testimony made before local government and a climate group he started, Rutinel has pressed the case that many climate advocates have articulated in the past: that livestock contribute to global emissions as a byproduct through their digestive systems.
The resurfaced paper brings a government-led approach to many of his vocalized positions.
In it, Rutinel argued that ranchers and animal farmers should be incentivized through government initiatives to transition to plant-based farming with either a carrot or a stick.

"Governments can require that agribusiness internalize the environmental, public health, and animal welfare costs of animal farms through regulations, mandates or taxes," Rutinel wrote, suggesting penalties for companies to make up for their production.
"But one food system policy idea has not received sufficient attention: the direct funding of farm transitions from concentrated animal feeding operations to plant-based operations," he added.
Rutinel also argued state and local governments could finance offsetting projects that would reduce emissions.

"For example, a manufacturing facility in California can decrease its net emissions by purchasing offset credits that finance a reforestation project in Brazil. Offset credits can be purchased voluntarily or to exceed emission allowances within a compliance market."

To some onlookers who have cast doubt on Rutinel's positions in the past, the statements appear to confirm that his position is further left on energy than many Democrats pushing aggressive climate initiatives through legislation like the Green New Deal.

"You have to be legitimately insane to look at the Green New Deal and think it doesn't go far enough. Meatless Manny's vision to ban ranching would not only lead to catastrophic job losses in Colorado but also cause a beef shortage across America," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
HOUSE REPUBLICANS SPLINTER OVER PESTICIDE PROVISION IN FARM BILL AS MAHA MOVEMENT FLEXES ITS MUSCLE
Rep. Manny Rutinel listens to a speaker during the general assembly at the Colorado State Capitol Building on Wednesday, April 23, 2025. (AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rutinel’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether he continues to believe that climate reform must, on some level, mean change for farming industries.
Having cleared the Democratic primary, Rutinel will face off against Rep. Gabe Evans in the state’s Nov. 3, 2026, general election.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Fetterman answers whether he'll cross the aisle to confirm Trump AG nominee Todd Blanche
summary: John Fetterman says he won't vote for Todd Blanche as attorney general, breaking from his pattern of often supporting Trump's DOJ and Cabinet picks.
story: Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports from Capitol Hill on the Senate Judiciary Committee advancing Todd Blanche's nomination to the full Senate. While Republican Sen. Susan Collins announces opposition, committee Republicans maintain general consensus to support President Donald Trump's nominee. The hearing features criticism from progressive Democrats, including Sen. Cory Booker, who challenged Blanche's record and past actions.
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said Wednesday he would not vote for acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to officially take over the role leading the Department of Justice.

During a Wednesday appearance on comedian Jon Stewart's podcast, Fetterman was pressed on Democrats' failure to use the Senate filibuster to block President Donald Trump's Cabinet nominees. The senator responded by claiming he would not vote for Blanche, who is Trump's choice for attorney general.
"Many of them I didn't vote for," Fetterman said, referring to Trump's Cabinet nominees.
JOHN FETTERMAN MAKES IT 'VERY CLEAR' THAT HE'S 'NOT GOING TO BE A REPUBLICAN' DESPITE DEM BACKLASH
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., recently expressed that he would not support Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general. (Fox News Digital)

"And if you're going to bring up Blanche, I'm not going to vote for him as well. There are some that I would vote for, and then there are many that I haven't because I just don't believe that's the right person for the job overall. I really try to call balls and strikes," he told Stewart.
Fetterman has been one of the Democratic senators most supportive of Trump's Cabinet nominees, voting "yea" to confirm half of his nominees, according to a Fox News Digital review.

He was the only Democrat to support Trump's previous choice for attorney general, Pam Bondi. He also helped push Markwayne Mullin, the newest Homeland Security secretary, over the line, casting the decisive vote to advance Mullin out of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, 8-7. Fetterman was again the only Democrat to vote for Mullin's confirmation, joining the 53 Senate Republicans to confirm Mullin in a 54-37 vote.

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., gestures to now former Sen. Markwayne Mullin, R-Okla., as they stand in an elevator during a vote at the U.S. Capitol on March 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Despite Fetterman supporting Trump's previous pick to head the Department of Justice, it appears the president will not be able to count on his vote this time around.
TRUMP AG PICK TODD BLANCHE FACES SENATE TEST IN FIRST MAJOR CONFIRMATION FIGHT SINCE GRAHAM’S DEATH

Bondi won her nomination from the Senate in a 54-46 vote. Todd Blanche will likely have at least two fewer votes than that tally, as Fetterman joins Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, in publicly expressing opposition to Blanche.
"Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation," Collins said Tuesday.
Collins notably voted to confirm Blanche as the assistant attorney general in March.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, said she will not vote to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Two other potential GOP holdouts – Sens. Bill Cassidy, R-La., and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, – are still undecided, according to The Hill.

A pair of Republicans who had previously opposed Blanche's nomination – Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C. – flipped to "yeas" after Blanche agreed to stop pursuing a planned anti-weaponization fund.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appears before a Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation hearing at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C., on July 15, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Senate Judiciary Committee voted to advance Blanche's nomination to the full Senate on a strict party line vote, 12-10.
Fox News Digital contacted the White House, the DOJ and Fetterman for further comment.

title: Trump told donors 'we need to elect JD,' source confirms, as he weighs Vance or Rubio in 2028
summary: President Donald Trump told Republican donors "we need to elect JD" in a private Oval Office meeting, a source confirmed to Fox News Digital.
story: Vice President JD Vance discusses the war in Iran, efforts to negotiate with the regime, criticism directed at Indiana Fever WNBA player Sophie Cunningham and the birth of his fourth child on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

President Donald Trump has publicly been coy about whether he might back Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio to succeed him in the White House, but private comments to donors suggest he might be leaning toward the man he already picked as his running mate in 2024.
"At the end of the day, we need to elect JD," Trump told donors privately during an Oval Office meeting roughly two weeks ago, sources told The Washington Post.
A source familiar confirmed to Fox News Digital the Post's reporting on Trump's remark.

While Post sources say the remark is not evidence Trump has made a choice between his VP or Rubio, a man he has handed many hats in his administration, it is a rare and previously unreported lean of his long-term thinking.
Trump made just one reference to Vance in his donor speech in Las Vegas on Wednesday night, hailing "the war on fraud led by our great Vice President JD Vance: He's doing a great job."
VANCE, CRUZ, HEAD TO IOWA ON 2026 MISSIONS AS 2028 GOP RACE TO SUCCEED TRUMP HEATS UP
President Donald Trump has yet to officially point to either Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio as his successor of choice in 2028. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House, Vance's office and the Republican National Committee for comment Thursday morning.

Despite Vance having won the 2024 running mate sweepstakes, Trump has also lavishly praised Rubio for his work in peacemaking efforts in Venezuela, Cuba and the Middle East, while simultaneously serving as national security advisor among his many leadership roles in the administration.
The president earlier this year declared that Rubio would go down as "the greatest secretary of state in history."
Trump has also promoted a Vance-Rubio ticket as "unstoppable" — stopping short of explicitly saying who should be at the top of the ticket.
Trump did say last year that Vance is "most likely" his heir, because "in all fairness, he's the vice president."
NEW POLL COMPLICATES VANCE’S STATUS AS TRUMP’S LIKELY 2028 HEIR APPARENT

Secretary of State Marco Rubio's wearing of hats of leadership in many Trump administration roles has put him in the foreground of President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance's Cabinet. (SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump joked at the White House Correspondents Dinner last month – rescheduled after dodging another assassination attempt earlier this spring – he would be running for president for a fourth in a troll to his critics, donning a Trump 2028
While Vance has demurred when questioned about 2028, he has built a political team of advisors who, if he runs as expected, would quickly build out a presidential campaign.
Rubio, who is crisscrossing the globe, does not have a similar group of political aides, and Rubio has said he will back Vance if the vice president launches a 2028 campaign.
Notably, Vance is the RNC's finance chair, ostensibly giving him the keys to the cash vault of more than $128 million cash on hand, according to the June Federal Elections Commission filing.

Regardless, Republican sources confirmed to Fox News earlier this year that a group of GOP donors supporting the secretary of state is quietly exploring ways to boost Rubio's political profile, which has not sat well with some in the president's political orbit.
VANCE CONFRONTED ABOUT 2028 AMBITIONS AFTER TRUMP TEASES 'DREAM TEAM' RUBIO TICKET
Vice President JD Vance, President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been in lockstep on every issue in this second Trump administration.

"Vice President Vance is the future of the Republican Party, and Marco Rubio is one of his closest friends in the administration," an operative in Trump's political orbit told Fox News Digital earlier this year.
"The divisive stories from some donors trying to cause chaos are not helpful," the operative, who asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely, emphasized.

Trump more recently questioned White House staff about the two possible contenders during a flight aboard Marine One, according to the Post. Although one adviser told the newspaper that Trump has privately settled on Vance as the Republican heir apparent, six other advisers and allies said they were not convinced that the president had made up his mind.

Those advisers noted that Trump sometimes gives different signals to different audiences and could change his position before the 2028 campaign begins. His aides also broadly expect him to delay any formal endorsement, in part to avoid diminishing his own influence during the remainder of his presidency.
DEMOCRATS BUILD MIDTERM MOMENTUM, BUT REPUBLICANS STILL IN DRIVER'S SEAT IN SENATE MAJORITY BATTLE

Vice President JD Vance, President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and War Secretary Pete Hegseth have managed multiple wars and peacemaking efforts around the globe during this administration. (Getty Images)

The dynamic resembles Trump’s 2024 search for a running mate, when Vance and Rubio were among the finalists. Advisers told the Post that Trump enjoys maintaining suspense around major political decisions and is reluctant to hand the spotlight to a potential successor too early.

Vance, meanwhile, has not announced whether he will run. He said in June that he planned to discuss his political future with his wife after the midterm elections and has maintained that he remains focused on serving as vice president.
People close to Vance previously told the Post that he intended to wait until after the birth of his fourth child before seriously considering a campaign. The child was born on July 19.

The 2026 midterms could shape the emerging succession contest. Republican losses could encourage additional candidates to enter the race and make it easier for them to criticize Trump’s administration or challenge his preferred successor. A strong performance, by contrast, could strengthen Trump’s ability to shape the 2028 field.

Vance has spent much of his vice presidency building relationships with Republican donors and activists. He is closely associated with the younger, populist wing of the MAGA coalition and has taken on political and policy assignments that have helped raise his profile.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rubio historically has had stronger ties to traditional Republican donors, while Vance has deeper support among the party’s newer populist base.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Fauci held in contempt as COVID cellphone lands in hands of Senate investigators
summary: Sen. Rand Paul's committee voted to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he invoked the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times at his hearing.
story: Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., believes that he has the votes to hold former chief medical advisor to the president Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt for invoking the Fifth Amendment, and he plans to immediately refer him to the DOJ if successful.

Senate Republicans moved to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress in their pursuit of forcing the former architect of the nation’s COVID-19 response to go on record about his actions leading up to and during the pandemic.

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted on sharp party lines to charge Fauci, the former chief medical advisor to the president, with contempt after he refused to answer questions from both sides of the aisle over fear of self-incrimination.

The move follows Fauci’s decision to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights more than 100 times during his hearing last week, which prompted the panel’s chair, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., to vow that he would face "repercussions" for not testifying, or at least how Paul envisioned.
FAUCI'S HHS IPHONE TURNED OVER TO SENATE INVESTIGATORS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci listens during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Fauci declined to answer questions, asserting his Fifth Amendment right. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Typically, once a contempt resolution passes by committee, it heads to the Senate floor for a full vote. However, Paul’s resolution allows that step to be skipped altogether and allows him to send the referral directly to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia.

But Paul wants the Department of Justice (DOJ) involved as soon as possible. There’s also the question whether Fauci’s pardon from former President Joe Biden protected him during the hearing, which Paul hopes to find answers to.
"It’s a good legal discussion, and we will make those legal points to DOJ in sending the referral over," Paul told Fox News Digital ahead of the hearing.
RAND PAUL PREDICTS FAUCI CONTEMPT VOTE WILL PASS, VOWS SWIFT DOJ REFERRAL
It’s another chapter in the feud between Paul and Fauci that has extended over the last several years since the onset of the pandemic.

Paul has accused the former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) director of funding "risky" research that led to an alleged lab leak of the COVID-19 virus in China and has demanded that he end up behind bars.
And in the background, a copy of Fauci’s pandemic-era cellphone is now in the possession of Senate Republican investigators.

Fox News Digital confirmed that the Robert F. Kennedy Jr.-led Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) sent over a copy of the phone to the Senate Homeland Security Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations chaired by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.
TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Senator Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky and chairman of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, speaks during a hearing in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. Anthony Fauci declined to testify in a Senate committee hearing on his role in the U.S. response to COVID-19, invoking his 5th Amendment rights. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
That committee falls under the umbrella of Paul’s Homeland Security panel, which also received a trove of over 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary before last week’s hearing.
It is unclear if Johnson and Paul have access to the information on the phone.
Meanwhile, across the marble expanse of the Capitol, Republican investigators in the House are cooking up their own probe into Fauci.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., previously signaled that he was not done with Fauci, either.

After the longtime public health official pleaded the Fifth Amendment during his Senate hearing, Comer questioned the validity of his preemptive pardon granted by President Joe Biden. He also said his committee would be questioning Fauci further, though he did not elaborate.

"If former President Biden’s blanket autopen pardon is valid, then Dr. Fauci has no right to refuse to answer questions," Comer said, noting his committee had done extensive work probing the autopen pardons. "Based on the release of Dr. Fauci’s diary, which should have been provided to the House Oversight Committee last Congress...we’ll be asking Dr. Fauci whether he stands by his previous testimony to our Committee."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: US pauses government operations in cartel-ridden Mexican state
summary: The U.S. said “due to a threat against American interests," U.S. government activities in Mexico's western Michoacan State "have been suspended."
story: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum strongly criticizes the U.S. government for its alleged involvement in the 2024 abduction of former Sinaloa Cartel boss 'El Mayo' Zambada. Sheinbaum explicitly states the U.S. lied about its participation, claiming a violation of Mexican sovereignty. This incident raises serious questions about diplomatic relations between the two nations and American intervention in Mexico.

The U.S. State Department said a "threat against American interests" forced the United States to suspend all of its government activities in a Mexican state where visitors face a risk of violence "from terrorist groups, cartels, gangs and criminal organizations."

The warning from the U.S. Embassy & Consulates in Mexico about the state of Michoacan, which is located west of Mexico City, includes a halt to the inspections of avocados required for their export, according to The Associated Press.

"Due to a threat against American interests, U.S. government activities in Michoacan State have been suspended as of August 5," the message read. "Reminder that the U.S. travel advisory designates Michoacan as a Level 4 ‘Do Not Travel’ area."

While the U.S. Embassy did not specify the nature of the threat in its security alert, Michoacan Gov. Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla said on social media that a temporary halt to avocado inspections was intended to safeguard workers following recent arrests linked to alleged extortion, the AP reported.
5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS
Members of the Civil Guard of Michoacan patrol a highway with armored vehicles after a wave of violence in Aguililla, Mexico, on Feb. 24, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

The western state of Michoacan is the leading exporter of avocados to the U.S. and has a high level of organized crime activity with at least four cartels — designated as terrorist organizations by the Trump administration — operating in the region. Besides trafficking drugs, cartels also make money through extortion, including in the avocado industry.
The State Department warns Americans to "exercise increased caution" throughout Mexico due to "terrorism, crime, and kidnapping."
For Michoacan state, it said, "There is a risk of violence in the state from terrorist groups, cartels, gangs and criminal organizations."

Michoacan State Security Secretary Antonio Cruz told the AP that one of the arrests mentioned by the governor was of "El Poncho," the alias of Alfonso Fernández Magallón, leader of a local cartel operating in the avocado-growing region around Los Reyes.
SINALOA CARTEL BOSS 'EL MAYO' SENTENCED TO LIFE, ORDERED TO PAY $15B IN DRUG TRAFFICKING PROFITS
Members of the self-defense group Pueblos Unidos carry out guard duties to protect avocado plantations from drug cartels in Ario de Rosales, Michoacan, Mexico, on July 8, 2021. (AFP via Getty Images)
U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson welcomed the arrest, which came over the weekend. The U.S. government had offered a $5 million reward.
Cruz said his department was unaware of any direct incidents involving the avocado inspectors. However, 300 security personnel were deployed to the Los Reyes area as a preventive measure.
The governor said the priority was to "ensure the security conditions necessary for these operations to resume normally," as has happened in the past.
In 2025, Mexico sold $3.65 billion worth of avocados to the United States, and in the first four months of this year, those exports rose by 35% compared to the same period in the previous year.

title: Trump's endorsement collides with $2M effort to oust House ally
summary: Trump's endorsement faces a major test as Rep. Andy Ogles battles Charlie Hatcher in Tennessee's 5th Congressional District Republican primary.
story: Rep. Andy Ogles spoke with Fox News Digital ahead of what's expected to be a high-stakes primary for Tennessee's 5th Congressional District.
A key congressional primary race will serve as a test of President Donald Trump's political weight on Thursday night.

Voters in Tennessee's 5th Congressional District are headed to the polls to decide between Trump-backed Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., and Republican Charlie Hatcher, the former state agriculture commissioner, who scored an 11th-hour endorsement from Gov. Bill Lee on Tuesday evening.

Ogles, one of Trump's most vocal allies in Congress, is seeking a third term representing the Middle Tennessee district, which includes part of the Nashville suburbs. Hatcher is the state's former Agriculture commissioner under Lee, and served as Tennessee State Veterinarian before that under both Democrat and Republican administrations.
"I'm not really surprised at all. You know, they're friends," Ogles said of Lee endorsing his rival.
GOP GOVERNOR ENDORSES CANDIDATE CHALLENGING TRUMP-BACKED CONGRESSMAN IN REPUBLICAN US HOUSE PRIMARY
President Donald Trump speaks during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland on July 31, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)
He argued that his endorsements, including Trump and House GOP leaders, prove that he's the more conservative choice in the race.

"The golden endorsement that anyone wants is that of President Trump's, which I have. And I think Trump has really done a good job of making sure that he's choosing conservatives in races, which is also why I have the endorsement of [House Speaker] Mike Johnson, you know, conservative stalwart. [House Judiciary Committee Chair] Jim Jordan has endorsed me," Ogles said.
"And so you just go down the list of my endorsements, it's that of the conservatives, whereas my opponent has less conservative folks, shall we say, endorsing him."
TOP TRUMP ALLY WARNS SUPER PAC BANKROLLED BY DEM BILLIONAIRE IS MEDDLING IN GOP PRIMARY

And having Trump's backing is not a small edge in deep red Tennessee, which Trump won by double digits in 2024. He bested Vice President Kamala Harris by roughly 18 points in Tennessee's 5th Congressional District that year.
But despite that and his incumbency advantage, Ogles has still faced a tough race this year with a clean energy super PAC spending more than $1 million to unseat him.
Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., walks through the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 3, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition super PAC spent roughly $1.3 million against Ogles and in favor of Hatcher. The group boasts billionaire Chris Larsen as a top donor, who also previously donated to Harris' presidential campaign.
Ogles is a member of the ultra-conservative House Freedom Caucus, whose members have built a reputation as being thorns in the side of House GOP leaders.
TRUMP-BACKED REPUBLICAN ADVANCES TO FACE VULNERABLE DEMOCRAT IN KEY HOUSE BATTLEGROUND

But Ogles, for the most part, has avoided that label. He instead acted as a key liaison between Johnson and his right flank on several pieces of legislation, which has apparently earned the Louisiana Republican's loyalty in response.

Johnson spoke in support of Ogles at a tele-rally on Tuesday night, warning that he was the best choice against Democrats who would take the country down a "dark, dangerous, deadly road to communism" should they win in November.

"I think everybody who's listening to our voices tonight understands we have a fateful midterm election coming up," Johnson said. "We have to keep and maintain and grow the republican majority in the House, and Andy Ogles is a key part of this majority."
The House speaker also lauded Ogles as one of his top negotiators on extending Trump's tax cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act earlier this year, as well as other measures.

"We're working with a one or two vote margin, and at the end of the day, when things are tight, Andy Ogles is one of the members who's a small handful of guys who helps deliver the vote," Johnson said. "He helps me, he's my agent on the floor, you know, he's making sure that we corral the votes and get these things done. So he has an outsized influence in Congress, and he's a critical member of this team."

House Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, speaks to members of the media after a meeting with House Republicans at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Lee said in a video released Tuesday night that he and Hatcher have been friends for 25 years and that he's "stood with President Trump since day one," touting him as a conservative with strong right-wing values.

Hatcher thanked Lee for his endorsement on Facebook and added, "In Congress, I will work hard, serve people, and get the job done by pursuing sensible, problem-solving solutions. I will defend our conservative values, support President Trump’s agenda, and fight to lower the cost of living for Tennessee families."

But despite Lee invoking Trump in his endorsement, the pair have notably split on a Republican primary race once before. Trump endorsed Republican Bobby Harshbarger for a state Senate seat over a Lee-backed incumbent in 2024. Harshbarger ultimately won, and Trump denounced Lee as a "RINO" in a Truth Social post afterward.

title: Inside America's laser revolution as the military nears big battlefield breakthrough
summary: The Army is nearing a contract for its first operational laser weapon system after successful testing, marking a major directed energy milestone.
story: Laser weapons are moving beyond the lab and into military operations. Center for Strategic and International Studies missile defense expert Tom Karako breaks down what's changed, what lasers can actually do, and why they won't replace missiles.

For decades, laser weapons have represented one of the Pentagon's most ambitious technological goals — promising to shoot down enemy drones and missiles at the speed of light without expending costly interceptors.
Now, after years of testing and false starts, the Army appears poised to take its biggest step yet toward making that vision a battlefield reality.

The Army is nearing a contract award for the Enduring High Energy Laser (E-HEL), a system that, if fielded as expected, would represent the service's first laser weapon to transition into a permanent operational capability.

The development comes as the Pentagon races to adapt to a new era of warfare in which inexpensive drones can overwhelm traditional air defenses and force militaries to expend missile interceptors costing hundreds of thousands — or even millions — of dollars. If fielded, the E-HEL would mark a significant step toward giving U.S. forces a new way to counter those threats without relying solely on costly kinetic weapons.
PENTAGON CONSOLIDATES DRONE OVERSIGHT AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PUSHES RAPID UNMANNED WARFARE EXPANSION
An anti-drone laser system trialed on a Stryker combat military vehicle with a machine gun aimed at the sky in Ukraine during a counteroffensive. (Michelle Ursi/Getty Images)

In July, Army acquisition chief Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano said the service was negotiating a contract with AeroVironment for the E-HEL, describing it as the Army's first program of record for a family of high-energy laser systems. He said the technology had shown "a lot of recent promise and capability" during testing at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico.
A source with knowledge of the program told Fox News Digital the Army is nearing a contract award, though negotiations are continuing and nothing has been finalized.
The Army's move is not happening in isolation.

In July, the Air Force disclosed it is using the compact laser weapon system at multiple locations overseas to defend against drones. The Navy, meanwhile, has spent years testing its high-energy laser with integrated optical-dazzler and surveillance (HELIOS) aboard destroyers, gradually integrating directed-energy weapons into fleet operations.
Together, the developments suggest the Pentagon may be entering a new phase for directed-energy weapons after decades of research and billions of dollars in investment.

The U.S. is not alone in pursuing the technology. Israel has begun deploying its Iron Beam laser air defense system — developed with significant U.S. support — to counter rockets, mortars and drones, while China has publicly showcased a growing range of military laser systems and counter-drone weapons as it expands its own directed-energy capabilities.

Even so, the War Department has spent decades pursuing laser weapons, with many early U.S. programs struggling with technical hurdles ranging from power generation and beam control to thermal management and reliability in operational environments.
Epirus' Leonidas counter-drone system sends out a high-powered microwave beam that stops drones in their tracks.

"It's not about the laser anymore," Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. "It's all these other things that make it workable as a weapon system" — from ensuring it can withstand dust, heat and bad weather to developing doctrine, training operators and maintaining the systems in the field.

And because laser beams can continue traveling well beyond their intended target, the military also must ensure they do not inadvertently illuminate satellites or other aircraft, one reason integrating the technology into everyday operations has proven more complicated than simply building a powerful laser.

The shift has been driven in large part by the rapid proliferation of inexpensive drones across battlefields in Ukraine, the Middle East and the Red Sea, forcing militaries to rethink how they defend against increasingly cheap aerial threats.
Even as lasers move closer to operational use, they are unlikely to replace traditional missile defenses.
Unlike missiles, which can travel over the horizon to engage distant threats, lasers are largely line-of-sight weapons, meaning they can only strike targets they can directly "see."
US DRAINS CRITICAL MISSILE STOCKPILES IN IRAN WAR AS YEARSLONG REBUILD LOOMS
"It's great for when that drone is coming in on top of you," Karako said. "But it's more difficult to be able to get past the horizon."

That means lasers are expected to become another layer of the Pentagon's air defense architecture rather than a replacement for kinetic interceptors. Missiles will still be needed to engage threats at long distances and in adverse conditions, while lasers are likely to be most effective against drones and other aerial threats that have already entered a defended area.

The unnamed company reportedly told attendees at the Army’s UAS and Launched Effects Summit that their aircraft was behind the mystery drones in New Jersey last year, according to the New York Post. (iStock)

The Army is also pursuing a next-generation counter-drone missile expected to cost less than $150,000 per interceptor, part of a broader effort to expand lower-cost options for defeating unmanned aircraft.

Lasers are only one piece of the Pentagon's broader directed-energy push. The military also is testing high-powered microwave systems such as Epirus' Leonidas, which are designed to defend against one of the battlefield's fastest-growing threats: swarms of inexpensive drones.
Rather than relying on a kinetic interceptor, high-powered microwaves use bursts of electromagnetic energy to disrupt the electronics of multiple nearby unmanned aircraft simultaneously.

The Pentagon also is investing in radio-frequency technologies capable of jamming communications between drones and their operators or interfering with satellite navigation signals, potentially causing unmanned aircraft to lose control.

title: Socialist frontrunner’s tradition-trashing holiday rants come back to bite her: ‘Worst of humanity comes out’
summary: Francesca Hong's resurfaced posts reveal complaints about Thanksgiving, Halloween and fireworks, drawing mockery in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race.
story: Fox News host Will Cain discusses Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong facing criticism for a 2020 social media post calling to ‘cancel Thanksgiving’ on ‘The Will Cain Show.’
Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong may be leading the Democratic gubernatorial primary, but resurfaced social media posts suggest she has a problem with some of America’s biggest holidays.

Hong, a dues-paying member of the Democratic Socialists of America, has recently drawn considerable flak for stating in a November 2020 post that the country should "cancel Thanksgiving" in order to "stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed Indegenous [sic.] folx and women." A comment she has since walked back amid backlash, claiming that it's her "favorite holiday."
Less discussed, however, are her complaints about other popular American holidays.

"I miss working in a restaurant every day...except on VDay," she posted on Valentine's Day 2022. "As if we weren't invisible enough to those who don't recognize the emotional & physical labor of service work, the worst of humanity comes out from folks 'celebrating' on another day capitalism tells you how to show love."

Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) (L) and influencer and left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker (C) stand with Wisconsin Gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong during a campaign rally for Hong on August 2, 2026. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images)
SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

Figures on the left have long challenged traditional holidays such as Thanksgiving, Independence Day and Columbus Day over their historical associations. But Hong’s yearslong trail of posts criticizing or dismissing several major celebrations is drawing fresh scrutiny as she campaigns to lead a swing-state battleground.
"I don't allow myself to work Halloween weekend or the day of," Hong wrote in 2019. "I would actually ask every single person in costume to leave."
Six years later, she made another post telling her followers that they could ask her anything but noting that the "only subject off limits is Halloween."
"Not my thing," she added.

Conservative and liberal commentators alike have posted pictures of the Grinch in response to Hong’s old posts, suggesting that she has a hatred of holidays. One anonymous user accused her of "grinchmaxxing."
DEMS PUT ON BLAST OVER POLL THAT SHOWS RECORD-LOW PATRIOTISM IN US: 'TEAR OUR SOCIETY APART'
Fireworks from the Freedom 250 Salute to America Independence Day celebration go off after delays due to a thunderstorm on July 5, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
Hong also doesn’t seem to be a fan of one of America’s most iconic holiday celebrations.
"Why isn't there a curfew on fireworks?" she wrote in the early morning hours of July 5, 2020.
"I do not enjoy fireworks," she said on June 29, 2019.

"If Francesca Hong had the explicit goal to attack storied institutions in order to turn off as many normal people as possible, she wouldn’t be doing anything different," Republican commentator Steve Guest wrote on social media.
BIDEN’S POSH VACATION ENCLAVE ROILED AS CHURCH AXES JULY 4 TRADITION OVER ‘WHITENESS’ DEBATE: ‘SPEWING LIES’
Gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong speaks on stage during the Wisconsin Democrats 2026 Convention on June 14, 2026, in Madison, Wisconsin. (Getty Images for WisDems)

Though some have claimed Hong has a distaste for Christmas, pointing to a post where she felt "slightly attacked" when someone changed her computer background to a Christmas tree, she has also made multiple posts celebrating the holiday.
Conservatives have long accused Democrats of waging a "war on Christmas," a charge liberals deny.
While many are poking fun at Hong for her distaste toward holidays, others find it relatable.
"Tbh this doesn’t make me dislike her at all, she has character," Las Vegas DSA member Val Thomason wrote on X. "Like ‘oh you know Fran, she hates holidays.’"

story: Republican candidate in Michigan primary, who beat Trump-backed Amir Hassan despite suspending his campaign a month earlier, speaks at state GOP event following shock victory. (Credit: WWMT)

A Michigan Republican who suspended his campaign, endorsed one of his opponents and then won the primary anyway is back on the trail — and promising to take the fight to Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet.

Tom Smith surfaced at a GOP unity brunch in Macomb County on Wednesday, when he declared that he was "running" for Michigan’s 8th Congressional District and told Republican activists he would need their help to unseat Rivet. "My name is Tom Smith, and I’m running for the 8th Congressional District to unseat communist comrade Rivet," Smith said at a Republican unity brunch in Macomb County. "And I’ll need your help to do it."
REPUBLICAN WHO REPORTEDLY DROPPED OUT DEFEATS TRUMP'S PICK IN KEY SWING-DISTRICT PRIMARY
Thomas Smith won his congressional primary in Michigan. (Tom Smith for Congress via Facebook)

"I look forward to working with Speaker Johnson and the entire Republican team to expand our House majority and advance President Trump’s America First agenda to lower costs for working families and make America affordable again," Smith said.
TRUMP-BACKED REPUBLICAN ADVANCES TO FACE VULNERABLE DEMOCRAT IN KEY HOUSE BATTLEGROUND
Donald Trump speaks to members of the media outside the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Monday, April 13, 2026. (Salwan Georges/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

After dropping out of the race last month, Smith put his support behind his contender in the race, Al Lemmo, who finished third in Tuesday's GOP primary behind Thomas and Trump-backed candidate Amir Hassan.

People complete their ballots. (REBECCA DROKE/AFP via Getty Images)

"I fell short last night. I make no excuse. It was a tough race," Hassan said in the video, which appeared to be recorded from his car. "I know what God has in store for me – something greater, even if I can't see it right now and don't understand."
He subsequently congratulated his opponents, told his supporters he "looked forward to seeing [them] again," and said that despite his loss, "it's still time to flip the eighth."

Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee is running for governor in the 2026 race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Bill Lee. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
