WEARABLE PATCH VIBRATES WHEN DANGER IS NEARBY
Gene.01 uses sensor-filled skin across its body to detect nearby people before physical contact occurs. (Generative Bionics)
How the Gene.01 humanoid robot senses workers

Gene.01 carries distributed sensors across its torso and limbs. The company says this smart skin detects touch, temperature, proximity and force at the same time. Proximity sensing gives the robot an early warning when someone enters the space around its body.

The basic idea feels familiar. You may feel heat near a stove and pull your hand away before touching the surface. In a similar way, Gene.01 can detect a nearby person before the person touches its sensor-covered body. That information gives the robot's control system a chance to respond before contact. It can also continue measuring force if contact happens.

However, Generative Bionics has not released detailed workplace safety data showing how the system performs during full industrial shifts. For now, the safety benefits remain company claims tied to a newly introduced platform.
Why proximity sensing could reduce robot collisions

Traditional factory robots often operate behind barriers to keep workers outside their range of motion. Humanoid robots create a different challenge. Companies want these machines to use tools and move through spaces built for people. That could place them closer to human workers.

Cameras can help a robot see someone approaching. However, a camera may lose sight of a person who stands too close or moves behind part of the robot. Full-body proximity sensing adds another source of information. The robot can detect activity near its torso or limbs without depending entirely on its view of the room.
HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT
The humanoid can sense touch, temperature, proximity and force while working alongside people. (Generative Bionics)
Workers can physically teach Gene.01 new tasks

Gene.01's sensors could also change how workers teach a humanoid robot. A person can guide the robot's arm through a movement while the system records the motion and force involved. This gives the robot information that a video demonstration may leave out.

For example, a video can show a robot where to place its hand. Yet the footage may not reveal how tightly the robot should grip an object. Too little pressure could cause the item to slip. Excessive force could damage it.

By moving Gene.01's arm directly, a worker can demonstrate the physical feel of the task. The company says this approach can help the robot learn how much force to apply. That could make robot training more accessible to experienced workers who understand the job but do not program robots.
What Physical AI means for Gene.01

Generative Bionics built Gene.01 around an approach it calls Physical AI. Under this approach, engineers develop the robot's body and movement controls as a connected system. They do not build the hardware first and treat the software as a separate layer added later.

The team uses models of the robot and its human partner. It can then adjust the design around measurable factors such as walking stability and physical strain on the person. The approach grew from research conducted by members of the company's founding team at the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia.

Nature Machine Intelligence published that research on July 13, 2026. The paper focuses on a human-aware robot called ergoCub rather than Gene.01. Researchers jointly optimized ergoCub's physical design and movement controls. They used human-related measurements, including stress on a person's back alongside the robot's walking requirements. Generative Bionics says Gene.01 is the first industrial platform to apply that peer-reviewed methodology to a fully functional humanoid covered in sensors.
Generative Bionics built Gene.01 in 6 months

The company says its team moved Gene.01 from a concept to a functional platform in six months. Generative Bionics CEO Daniele Pucci said the company designed the robot as a foundation for different industrial machines.

"Unlike other one-size-fits-all humanoids, Gene.01 is a scalable platform, customized at the edge of AI, design and end-effector level to maximize each customer's needs. It is also the first expression of our belief that physical AI must be human-aware, physics-native and industrial from day one. In six months, our team moved from concept to a fully functional and sensorized humanoid platform by combining deep humanoid robotics expertise with AI, biomechanics and design."
Pucci said the company wants robots to learn from the physical world while adapting to each customer's work.
Workers can guide Gene.01’s hands directly to teach movements and the amount of force a task requires. (Generative Bionics)
Gene.01 can change for different industrial jobs

Generative Bionics designed Gene.01 as a base for a family of specialized humanoids. The company can adjust the AI for a particular task. It can also alter the robot's exterior to fit the working environment.

Meanwhile, engineers can replace its end effectors. That technical term covers the hands, grippers or feet attached to the ends of a robot's limbs. A robot built for warehouse work may need a different hand than one designed to operate welding equipment. This platform approach lets Generative Bionics adapt one core robot instead of designing every machine from the ground up.

The company sees potential uses in manufacturing and logistics. It has also identified inspection, public safety and health care as possible future markets. However, Gene.01 remains an early industrial platform. Generative Bionics still needs to show that its customization strategy can work reliably outside controlled demonstrations.
An open-source Gene.01 model gives developers a head start

Generative Bionics has also started releasing a digital model of Gene.01. The model lets developers simulate the robot before they gain access to the physical machine. They can test movement software and begin developing industry-specific applications in a virtual environment.

The company's website currently links to a preview of the robot's URDF model on GitHub. URDF stands for unified robot description format. Developers use it to describe a robot's physical structure for software and simulation tools. Generative Bionics says it wants to maintain the model across software distribution systems that physical AI developers already use. An open model could attract researchers and robotics developers to the platform.
Fincantieri partnership targets shipyard welding

Gene.01's first planned industrial use involves shipbuilding. Generative Bionics is working with Italian shipbuilding company Fincantieri to develop a humanoid for welding operations in shipyards. Shipyards can contain tight work areas and heavy equipment. Welding also exposes workers to heat and fumes. A humanoid could eventually handle selected tasks in areas that place extra physical demands on people. However, Generative Bionics and Fincantieri have not yet published detailed performance results from the welding project. The partnership will give Gene.01 an important test.
Generative Bionics built Gene.01 as a customizable platform for industrial jobs, including a planned shipyard welding application. (Generative Bionics)
An $81M investment backs the robot company

Generative Bionics has raised an $81 million seed round led by CDP Venture Capital. AMD Ventures, Duferco and Eni Next participated in the round. RoboIT and Tether also invested. That funding gives the company more resources to develop Gene.01 and expand its production capacity. Generative Bionics says its team includes about 100 people. Nearly half hold doctoral degrees, according to the company. The team's experience includes earlier humanoid projects such as iCub and ergoCub.
Generative Bionics wants a European robot supply chain

The company also wants to build more of its humanoid technology in Europe. Generative Bionics formed a strategic partnership with German company Synapticon to develop an actuation system for Gene.01 and future robots. Actuators serve as the motorized joints that move a robot's body. They play an important role in how quickly and forcefully a humanoid can move. The partnership covers final assembly and calibration in Europe. The companies also plan to conduct safety testing there. Generative Bionics says this approach will give it more control over key components while supporting European compliance requirements.
What the Gene.01 humanoid robot means for you

You probably will not find Gene.01 working beside you tomorrow. Still, its sensing skin points to a larger change in humanoid robot design. Companies want these machines to move beyond fenced-off areas and enter workplaces built for people. To do that safely, robots need more awareness of the humans standing around them. Detecting a worker before contact gives the machine more time to react. Force sensing could also help the robot respond more carefully when physical interaction occurs.
Kurt's key takeaways

Gene.01 introduces a promising idea for factory safety. Its sensor-filled skin can detect a nearby person before physical contact and continue measuring force during an interaction. The system could also help workers teach the robot by physically guiding its movements. That gives Gene.01 information about force that video demonstrations may miss. However, most of the performance and safety details currently come from Generative Bionics. The company now needs to support those claims with workplace testing and clear data. Smart skin may give a humanoid more awareness of the person beside it. Yet awareness only helps when the robot reacts correctly every time.
Would you trust smart skin to protect you from a full-size humanoid at work, or would you still want a barrier between you and the machine? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Paidwork breach exposes 23M user records
summary: The Paidwork data breach exposed 23 million accounts including bank account numbers, addresses and password hashes from the microtask platform.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Making a few extra dollars online should not put your bank details or identity at risk. Yet that is the concern for people who used Paidwork, an online earnings application.
A leaked database tied to the platform reportedly contains information from more than 23 million accounts. If you ever signed up, now is a good time to take the warning seriously.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
COULD THE 7-ELEVEN BREACH AFFECT YOU?

Paidwork lets people earn small amounts through online microtasks, but the reported breach shows how much personal information can sit behind those tiny payouts. (Photo by Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
What happened in the Paidwork data breach

Paidwork is a microtask platform that offers small payments for completing online activities. Those jobs can include answering surveys, testing apps and watching advertisements. You complete tasks, build a balance and eventually request a payout. For many people, the account may feel low risk because the earnings are small. However, the information behind those payments can be far more valuable.

Hackers claimed in March 2026 that they had obtained data from Paidwork. They later offered the information for sale. Nearly 11 GB of data allegedly taken from the platform appeared publicly in July. The data breach notification service Have I Been Pwned analyzed the released files and found more than 23 million unique email addresses. The service added the incident to its database on July 19, 2026.
Paidwork told CyberGuy it is actively investigating the reported breach, working with external security specialists and taking steps to protect affected accounts and notify users as appropriate.
What information the Paidwork leak reportedly exposed

The exposed information appears to reach far beyond email addresses. Have I Been Pwned says the files contain names, phone numbers, physical addresses and dates of birth. They also reportedly include education levels, gender information, profile photos and personal interests.

The financial records raise additional concern. The files reportedly contain bank account numbers, transaction information and payout histories. Attackers may also have device information and IP addresses. Those details can reveal how you connected to the service and which equipment you used.

Finally, the leak reportedly contains passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. Bcrypt makes passwords harder to crack than weaker storage methods. However, short or predictable passwords can still face attacks. That is a huge amount of personal information to exchange for tasks that may pay only a few cents.
WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME

The leaked database reportedly includes names, home addresses, bank details, transaction records and password hashes tied to more than 23 million accounts. (Photo by Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)
Why the Paidwork breach could follow you for years

You may have earned very little through Paidwork. A criminal could still find plenty of value in your account. For example, a phishing email could mention a real payout before claiming that your bank transfer failed. Another message could include your address to make a fake security warning look convincing.

Criminals can combine several leaked details to build a believable story around you. Password reuse creates another danger. If attackers crack your Paidwork password, they can test it on other websites. This type of attack is called credential stuffing. It succeeds when people reuse one password across several accounts. Your email account should cause the greatest concern. Someone who gets inside may use it to reset passwords for other services.

Bank account numbers and transaction histories can also support convincing fraud attempts. A caller who knows your payment history may sound like a legitimate representative. Attackers do not care how much you earned. They care how much they can make from the information connected to you.
Why earning pennies can put valuable data at risk

This leak should make all of us think carefully about the information we give side-income platforms. A task may pay only a few cents. Meanwhile, the service may request your legal name and bank account information before releasing your earnings.

It may also collect your birth date, home address or information about your device. That creates an uneven trade. Before joining an earning app, review what information it collects. Look for an explanation of why the company needs each detail.

Also, check whether you can delete your account after you stop using the platform. Find out whether you can remove old payout methods and profile information. Avoid completing optional profile fields that reveal extra details about your life. The company cannot lose information that you never provided. You should also think carefully before connecting your primary bank account to a service you plan to use only occasionally.
Anyone who used Paidwork should change reused passwords, watch financial accounts and stay alert for phishing messages built with stolen personal details. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to check for your information in the Paidwork breach
Have I Been Pwned lists the Paidwork incident as affecting 23.3 million accounts. You can search the email address you used for the platform through its breach-checking tool.

A match means your email address appears in the released files. However, the public search will not display every exposed detail connected to you. You should still secure your accounts when a search produces no match. Public breach databases may contain incomplete records.

Also, make sure you visit the real Have I Been Pwned website. Criminals often create fake breach-checking pages to collect more personal information. Never enter a password, Social Security number or banking information into a breach-search tool.
Ways to stay safe after the Paidwork data breach
Start with your login credentials and financial accounts. Then reduce the amount of personal information criminals can find elsewhere.

To see if your email was affected, visit Have I Been Pwned at haveibeenpwned.com . It is the first and official source for this newly added dataset. Enter your email address to find out if your information appears in the Synthient leak. When done, come back here for Step 2.

Change the password connected to your Paidwork account, even if you no longer use the platform. Create a completely new password. Avoid adding a symbol or number to your old password because criminals often test common variations. Next, change that password on every other account where you reused it. Also, immediately replace an exposed password anywhere you used it.

A password manager can create and store a different password for each account. That limits the damage from one exposed login. You also avoid relying on short passwords that are easier to remember and crack. Protect the password manager with a strong master password. Then enable multifactor authentication for the password manager itself.

Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) anywhere the option appears. Start with your email account. Then protect your bank, payment services and other important accounts. An authenticator app or security key usually provides stronger protection than a text message. However, any second verification step can improve your security.

Contact any bank or payment service you connected to Paidwork. Explain that your account information may appear in a leaked database. Ask whether the institution recommends extra monitoring or a replacement account number. Next, turn on alerts for withdrawals and transfers. You should also receive a warning when someone changes your account information. Report any transaction that you do not recognize. Do not ignore a small charge because criminals sometimes use minor transactions to test an account.

A credit freeze can help stop someone from opening a new credit account in your name. You need to place the freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze costs nothing to place or remove. You do not need to wait for evidence of identity theft. The FTC says a credit freeze can help after your personal information appears in a data breach. Remember that a credit freeze cannot prevent fraud involving an account you already have. Continue watching your existing bank and credit card statements.

Be suspicious of emails, texts or calls that mention Paidwork, a payout or a bank transfer. A criminal may know your full name or address. That knowledge does not prove the message came from a legitimate company. Avoid clicking links in unexpected messages. Open the official app or type the company's address into your browser instead. Never share a verification code with someone who contacts you. Criminals often request those codes while trying to enter your account. Phishing links can steal information or install malware on your device.

Strong antivirus software can warn you about malicious links, infected attachments and fake websites. This protection becomes especially useful after a breach. Criminals often send fake security alerts that pressure you to download a file or visit a login page. Keep your security software updated so it can recognize newer threats. However, antivirus protection cannot catch every convincing scam. Continue checking the sender and web address before clicking anything. The FTC recommends using security software to protect your devices from malware and other online threats. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

The Paidwork files reportedly contain information that may also appear on people-search websites. A data removal service can send opt-out requests to data brokers that collect and sell personal information. Reducing those records may make it harder for criminals to expand a leaked profile. You can also submit the removal requests yourself for free. However, you may need to contact many sites and repeat the process when your information returns. A data removal service cannot erase the Paidwork files from criminal forums. It also cannot remove government records or every old listing from the internet. The FTC says people-search sites usually provide an opt-out process. It also notes that paid services can complete requests on your behalf. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

A platform may pay you a few cents while storing information that can affect your life for years. The Paidwork files reportedly combine personal profiles with banking information and password hashes. That gives criminals several ways to target you, even when your Paidwork balance was nearly empty. Paidwork says it has no confirmed evidence its systems or accounts were compromised. However, Have I Been Pwned found more than 23 million unique email addresses in the publicly released files. Treat the warning seriously if you ever used the platform. Change reused passwords first. Then secure your financial accounts and watch for messages that know a little too much about you.
How much personal information should a side-hustle platform be allowed to collect for a few dollars in return? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Foreign robot ban targets China over security fears
summary: The FCC added foreign-produced humanoid robots and connected power inverters to its Covered List, blocking new models from receiving U.S. authorization.
story: Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, introduces the bipartisan Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026, aiming to effectively block Chinese-made electric vehicles from the U.S. market. Moreno warns against these vehicles, saying they could potentially allow remote control and pose significant national security threats. He emphasizes protecting the American auto industry and workers from subsidized Chinese exports.

A humanoid robot can carry equipment through a factory or help researchers test new artificial intelligence. However, its cameras can watch everything nearby. Its internet connection can also send valuable information beyond the building. The Trump administration now sees that combination as a potential national security problem.

On July 28, the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-produced advanced robots and connected power inverters to its Covered List. The action blocks many new models from receiving the FCC authorization required before companies can import or sell them in the United States.

Although the final language applies broadly to foreign-produced equipment, China reportedly sits at the center of the crackdown. Officials want to prevent surveillance and cyberattacks while reducing America's reliance on Chinese technology. They also hope companies will move more manufacturing to the United States.
HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
The FCC is blocking new foreign-made advanced robots and connected power inverters over cybersecurity and national security concerns. (Tang Yanjun/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images)
Why the foreign robot ban is happening now

Humanoid robots are no longer limited to flashy demonstrations that rack up views online. Companies are preparing them for factories and warehouses. Researchers are also testing them inside laboratories. Four-legged robots can inspect dangerous areas or patrol large properties. Meanwhile, robot developers are building new safety systems as these machines begin working closer to people.

That sounds useful, but these machines also see and hear a lot. Many come equipped with cameras and microphones. Other sensors help them map rooms, recognize objects and respond to people. The robot may connect to cloud services for AI processing. A company might also use that connection to install software updates or provide remote support. That connection is where the FCC sees a potential problem.

If a hacker gets inside the system, the robot could collect sensitive information or send data somewhere it should not go. An attacker might also interfere with its movements. In some cases, that person could gain remote control. We have already seen how those risks can surface in ordinary connected machines. A recent security report involving Yarbo robot mowers raised concerns about remote access, live camera feeds and saved Wi-Fi information.

Now think about a more powerful robot working inside a factory or research lab. Federal national security agencies say some foreign-made robots could create unacceptable cybersecurity and supply chain risks. They worry that hostile governments could use the technology to monitor Americans. The machines could also gather intelligence from sensitive locations. A stolen password is bad enough. A hacked robot can move through a building while recording what it sees. It may also operate close to valuable equipment.
How the FCC foreign robot ban works

The FCC did not tell Americans to surrender robots they already own. The government also did not automatically order retailers to remove every foreign robot from store shelves. Instead, the agency added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to its Covered List.

Equipment on that list generally cannot receive a new FCC authorization. Most connected electronic products need that approval before companies can import, market or sell them in the United States. As a result, the restrictions mainly affect new models that have not received authorization. Previously approved products can remain available, although the FCC reportedly retains the authority to revoke earlier approvals.

Companies may also seek conditional approval. Federal national security agencies can review a device and decide whether it presents an acceptable level of risk. Officials expect many non-Chinese suppliers to reportedly receive exemptions. That suggests the broader foreign-made restriction will hit Chinese manufacturers the hardest.

This move did not come out of nowhere. Lawmakers had already introduced a bipartisan proposal that would block federal agencies from using certain robots tied to foreign adversaries. The latest FCC action reaches much further because it can prevent new products from entering the broader American market.
Why power inverters are included in the crackdown

Power inverters rarely attract the same attention as walking robots. Still, they play an important role in America's energy system. An inverter converts direct current electricity into alternating current electricity. Solar panels and batteries generate or store direct current. Homes, power grids and data centers generally need alternating current.

Many inverters today connect to the internet. Operators use those connections to check performance and install updates. Some systems also allow remote adjustments. However, remote access creates another potential doorway for attackers.

Federal officials worry that foreign companies or hackers could interfere with connected inverters. A coordinated attack might disrupt equipment or expose information about how energy moves through a facility.

A major interruption could affect internet cloud services and the businesses that rely on them. An inverter may look like a metal box mounted beside a solar array. Still, when thousands of connected units feed electricity into important systems, their security becomes much harder to ignore.
OHIO ROBOT COP RETIRES AFTER ZERO ARRESTS
New FCC restrictions could hit Chinese robotics companies hardest while limiting access to lower-cost machines used by U.S. researchers. (REUTERS/Tingshu Wang)
Why China sits at the center of the robot fight

Chinese companies have become major players in advanced robotics. They have gained attention by offering capable machines at prices that U.S. developers may struggle to match. The ban could reportedly hit Unitree especially hard. Counterpoint Research estimates that the Chinese company holds just under one-fifth of the global humanoid robot market.

Unitree has also worked with Nvidia to use its Blackwell AI chips in a robot platform. Nvidia has said data from those robots will remain in the United States. The company also said many Unitree customers in America are universities and research institutions. China strongly criticized the FCC action. Its embassy in Washington accused the United States of unfairly targeting Chinese businesses. It also warned that Beijing could respond if the restrictions harm Chinese interests. Meanwhile, China's Foreign Ministry called the policy protectionist. A spokesperson argued that the restrictions could hurt American companies and consumers. We reached out to Unitree for comment, but did not hear back before our deadline.
Could the robot ban slow American innovation?

The foreign robot ban may give U.S. manufacturers more room to grow. American companies will face less competition from low-cost Chinese machines in the domestic market. However, the policy could create short-term problems for researchers and startups. Some American teams use affordable Chinese robots to test software or train AI systems. Losing access to newer models could raise costs and limit the hardware available for experiments.

The restrictions could also complicate partnerships between U.S. chipmakers and Chinese robotics companies. That may slow certain projects even as Washington tries to strengthen domestic production. The bigger question involves timing. Building a competitive American robotics supply chain will take investment and skilled workers. Manufacturers must also secure motors, sensors and other components. Until that happens, tighter restrictions could leave a gap between the robots American developers want and the machines they can afford.
How to protect yourself when buying a connected robot

You may never bring a humanoid robot into your home, but smaller connected robots are already everywhere. Robot vacuums, lawn mowers and security devices can collect video, map your property and connect to remote servers. Before you buy one, take a few minutes to check how the company protects that access.

Connected devices sold in the United States should include an FCC identification number. You can usually find it on the product, packaging or manufacturer's website. Be cautious if the company provides no clear regulatory information.
Find out whether the robot stores camera footage and room maps locally or uploads them to the cloud. The privacy policy should explain where the company stores that information and who can access it.
Turn off remote viewing or cloud controls when you do not need them. A feature that lets you control a robot from anywhere could also become an entry point for someone else.
TOP TRUMP AGENCY PURGES OVER 20 SUSPECTED CHINA-LINKED PRODUCTS FROM FEDERAL MARKETPLACE
Washington is targeting foreign-produced robots that can collect video, map sensitive locations and connect to remote cloud systems. (ADEK BERRY / AFP via Getty Images)
Robot software needs updates just like your phone or computer. Enable automatic updates when available and avoid products from companies with a poor support record.
Place connected robots and other smart devices on a guest network when your router supports it. That can help keep a compromised device away from your computers and sensitive files.

Use a strong, unique password for the account that controls your robot. A password manager can create and securely store it for you. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) if the manufacturer offers it.

If you are installing a connected solar or battery inverter, ask the installer who can access it remotely. You should also find out how the company handles software updates and what happens if its online service shuts down.
Kurt's key takeaways

I understand why Washington is paying close attention to this. A network-connected machine with cameras and powerful motors warrants a thorough security review. That concern grows when the robot enters a factory, research center or part of America's energy infrastructure. At the same time, banning new foreign models creates a real tradeoff. Chinese companies currently build many advanced robots at prices American researchers can afford. Restricting that hardware may protect sensitive systems, but it could also slow some U.S. innovation while domestic manufacturers catch up. The success of this policy will depend on what comes next. America needs secure products, strong testing and enough domestic production to give buyers a genuine choice.
Would you accept fewer robot choices and potentially higher prices if the government said the restrictions could prevent foreign surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: AI models accessed systems of 3 real organizations, company reveals
summary: Stay up to date on the latest AI technology advancements and learn about the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
story: Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei speaks at the How AI Will Transform Business in the Next 18 Months panel during Inbound 2025 Powered by HubSpot at Moscone Center Sept. 4, 2025, in San Francisco. (Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot))
IN TODAY'S NEWSLETTER:
- Anthropic says AI models accessed systems of 3 real organizations during testing
- How AI could redefine healthcare by the end of the decade
- Fox News Poll finds voters hitting the brakes on data centers

MIND OF ITS OWN: Anthropic announced Thursday that three of its artificial intelligence models accessed the open internet during cybersecurity testing and gained unauthorized access to the systems of three real organizations.

SHOT IN THE ARM: Advances in artificial intelligence will help reshape the healthcare industry in the years ahead, a new report finds. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the largest group of technical professionals that's dedicated to advancing technology to benefit humanity, released its Technology Megatrends 2030 Report Wednesday after it was reviewed exclusively by FOX Business.
AI advances will redefine the healthcare industry by 2030, a report finds. (iStock)

SWITCHED OFF: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Tuesday added foreign-produced power inverters and advanced robotic devices to its covered list, generally making new models ineligible for FCC equipment authorization after U.S. national security agencies determined the products pose unacceptable risks to America's critical infrastructure and supply chains.

FUTURE TECH: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote in a new op-ed published on Tuesday that the rise of artificial intelligence should be used to empower all people rather than being centralized and controlled by a few institutions.

DRAWING THE LINE: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushed back on claims his AI startup supports a ban on open-weight models to support its competitive position in a letter after Anthropic was notably absent from a letter signed by many leading AI firms.

LABOR LIFT: A facilities management company is investing $200,000 in artificial intelligence to help skilled trades workers become more productive. New Jersey-based NEST Integrated Facilities Management announced last week that it is partnering with Saint Joseph’s University in Philadelphia on "The Hawk’s NEST: Building the Future of IFM and Skilled Trades Intelligence."

PLUG PULLED: While U.S. tech companies race for AI dominance, the latest Fox News nationwide survey finds voters hitting the brakes on data centers as more prefer taking time to address local concerns than rushing expansion to maintain a competitive global edge.

EYES ON YOU: Would you wear a small AI device that periodically looks at you and studies the world around you? A Singapore-based smart hardware and AI company, Lingverse, is betting people may be ready for that level of attention. Lingverse has raised $29 million to develop an AI wearable called iKairos. The company describes it as a personal AI guardian that can offer help before you ask.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wears the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses as he delivers a speech presenting the new line of smart glasses during the Meta Connect event at the company's headquarters in Menlo Park, Calif, Sept. 17, 2025. (Reuters/Carlos Barria)

OPINION: Imagine if, during World War II, protesters had gathered outside factories making tanks and planes and tried to shut them down. Or that just before Pearl Harbor, when American industry was "hyperscaling" its defense infrastructure to make the country ready for war, cities and counties had placed restrictions on new plant and shipyard openings and tried to dictate what could be produced where — as long as it wasn’t near them.

LAND OF THE FREE: Willie Nelson urged Americans to think again when it comes to building the future. Nelson, 93, encouraged followers to "fight against data centers invading our land" in a social media plea shared Tuesday.

title: KARR Bluetooth flaw exposes 2.2M cars to theft risk
summary: A Bluetooth vulnerability in dealer-installed KARR and SWDS security devices puts 2.2 million vehicles at risk of being unlocked by nearby attackers.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Could a small device hidden beneath your dashboard make your car easier to break into? Nancy from Newtown, Pennsylvania, asked me where she should look for the KARR or SWDS "code" in her 2025 Cadillac XT5 and 2024 Hyundai Tucson Limited Hybrid.

Here is the first thing you need to know. There is no code to find in your vehicle's settings. KARR and SWDS refer to aftermarket security hardware that a dealership may have installed before selling the car. SWDS stands for Southwest Dealer Services, the company associated with several KARR-branded vehicle protection products.
The device usually sits beneath the dashboard on the driver's side. You may also find a KARR or SWDS sticker on the driver-side window.
So, before you start searching through menus or calling the automaker, here is how to find out whether your vehicle has one of these devices and what to do next.
15 SECURITY ESSENTIALS TO KEEP YOUR VALUABLES SAFE FOR SUMMER TRAVEL

A Bluetooth flaw in dealer-installed KARR and SWDS security devices could expose about 2.2 million vehicles to unauthorized access. (David Baillot/University of California San Diego/Jacobs School of Engineering)
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
KARR Bluetooth car hack puts 2.2 million vehicles at risk

Computer security researchers at the University of California San Diego uncovered a Bluetooth vulnerability affecting at least 2.2 million vehicles. The flaw involves dealer-installed KARR and SWDS security devices. A person standing within about five yards of a vulnerable vehicle could connect to the device through Bluetooth.

From there, an attacker could lock or unlock the doors. The same flaw could silence the alarm, sound the horn or flash the headlights. An attacker could also prevent a parked vehicle from starting. However, the researchers did not report that the flaw could start the engine or shut down a vehicle that was already running. That distinction is important. The Bluetooth flaw alone does not let someone drive away. However, it could quietly unlock the doors. A thief could then use separate tools to create or program a key.
What are KARR and SWDS car security systems?

KARR systems are aftermarket vehicle security products sold through participating dealerships. They may include an alarm, GPS tracking, remote vehicle controls or an ignition-disabling feature. Southwest Dealer Services uses several product names, including KARR Security, KARR Fusion, KARR BT, KARR S.W.A.T. and S.W.A.T. Dealer. The features vary by product and vehicle.

These devices do not come from Cadillac, Hyundai, Ford or another automaker's factory. A dealership or one of its vendors adds the hardware after the vehicle arrives. Dealers may use the system to protect inventory sitting on the lot. When someone buys the vehicle, the dealer may offer the system as an additional security package. The problem is that some dealers left the hardware connected even when buyers declined the service. As a result, a driver might have a vulnerable device without an active KARR account or any idea that the equipment is inside the car.
How the KARR Bluetooth vulnerability works

The KARR device communicates with a smartphone app through Bluetooth Low Energy. Researchers found that the affected devices relied on the same secret authentication key. Once they recovered that key, they could send commands that vulnerable KARR devices accepted.

Think of it as giving a huge group of devices the same unchangeable password. Once that password becomes known, each device becomes easier to approach. The researchers also found that the devices broadcast recognizable Bluetooth signals. Historical databases containing those signals could reveal where a particular device had appeared. That creates a privacy concern beyond car theft. Someone could potentially use the data to study where a vehicle regularly parks or travels.
Which cars may have a KARR or SWDS device?

UC San Diego researchers found the devices most often in vehicles sold through Honda, Toyota, Mazda, Ford and Jeep dealerships in Southern California since 2017. However, that list does not mean other brands are safe.

KARR works with more than 3,000 dealerships nationwide. Vehicles also move around the country through used-car sales, auctions and dealership trades. Therefore, the vehicle's make and model cannot confirm whether it has the equipment. The dealership that prepared the vehicle for sale matters more than the badge on the grille. A Cadillac, Hyundai or Chevrolet could have a KARR system if the selling dealer installed one. A Honda from another dealership might never have received it.
How to check your car for a hidden KARR device
Start with the easy clues before you remove any trim or crawl too far beneath the dashboard.
Look at the lower corners and edges of the driver-side window.
The sticker may say:
KARRKARR Security SystemsSWDSS.W.A.T.
KARR
KARR Security Systems
SWDS
S.W.A.T.

A sticker strongly suggests that the dealership installed a related device. However, the absence of a sticker cannot completely clear your vehicle. A dealer or previous owner may have removed the label while leaving the hardware connected. UC San Diego says many affected vehicles have the sticker, rather than every affected vehicle.

Park the vehicle and shut off the engine. Move the driver's seat back and use a flashlight to look beneath the lower dashboard. Researchers say the device is usually installed underneath the dashboard on the driver's side.

You may see a small button or indicator light attached to the bottom edge of the dash. Wiring may run from the button behind the dashboard panels. The button shown by UC San Diego is small and easy to miss. It can look like a basic aftermarket alarm switch rather than a modern connected device. Do not pull on the wires or disconnect anything. The module may connect to the ignition system and other vehicle electronics.
Check the purchase agreement, dealer addendum, finance documents and service records.
Search for references to:
KARR SecurityKARR BTKARR FusionKARR S.W.A.T.SWDSSouthwest Dealer ServicesDealer alarmVehicle recovery systemInventory security system
KARR Security
KARR BT
KARR Fusion
KARR S.W.A.T.
SWDS
Southwest Dealer Services
Dealer alarm
Vehicle recovery system
Inventory security system
The charge may appear as part of a larger dealer protection package. You may also find the product listed with no separate price if the dealer installed it for inventory control.
TESLA HELPED SAVE A DRIVER; IS YOUR CAR READY?
Some Jeep, Ram and Chrysler drivers previously saw promotional messages on infotainment screens through Stellantis’ Uconnect system. (Kurt "Cyberguy" Knutsson)

Call the dealership that originally sold the vehicle. This step can help even when you bought the car used from another business. Your VIN appears near the bottom of the windshield on the driver's side. You can also find it on the registration, insurance card and driver-side door frame.
Ask the dealer: "Can you check this VIN and confirm whether your dealership or inventory vendor installed a KARR, SWDS, KARR BT, S.W.A.T. or other aftermarket security module?"

Then ask these follow-up questions: "Is the device still connected?" "Has it received the firmware update released on July 20, 2026?" "Can you provide the device model and firmware status in writing?"
A vague answer such as "Your factory alarm is fine" does not address the question. You are asking about dealer-installed aftermarket equipment.

KARR says people who never activated the security service can still use the official KARR Security app to check their VIN. Download the app only through the official Apple App Store, Google Play Store or KARR website. Do not use an app link from an unexpected text message, email or online advertisement.

After opening the app near the vehicle, tap the customer service link at the bottom of the screen. The app should guide you through the VIN check and available firmware update. KARR also lists customer support at 800-395-5277.
What Nancy should check on her Cadillac and Hyundai

Nancy's 2025 Cadillac XT5 and 2024 Hyundai Tucson Limited Hybrid were not among the specific brands UC San Diego researchers said appeared most often. However, that does not rule them out. The device comes from the dealership rather than Cadillac or Hyundai.

Nancy should check each SUV separately. First, she should look for a KARR or SWDS sticker on the driver-side window. Next, she should use a flashlight to inspect the lower edge of the dashboard near the driver's knees.

She should also review the paperwork from each dealership. If the vehicles came from different dealers, one could have the equipment while the other does not. Finally, Nancy should call both selling dealers with the VINs. She should ask whether either dealership installed a KARR, SWDS or S.W.A.T. module before delivery. If the dealers cannot provide a definite answer, she can use the official KARR app or call KARR support.
How to update a KARR security system

Acrisure released a firmware patch on July 20, 2026, one day before UC San Diego publicly announced the vulnerability. The vehicle owner must deliver the update to the KARR device through the official KARR Security app. Updating your phone or vehicle infotainment system will not patch the separate module.
An activated system means you purchased or activated KARR service through the dealership.
Follow these steps:

Go to the vehicle and sit in the driver's seat.Open the KARR Security app.Log in and select the correct vehicle.Tap the Settings button in the lower-right corner.Scroll down and tap Check for Updates.Follow the instructions shown in the app.Wait for confirmation that the firmware is current.
Go to the vehicle and sit in the driver's seat.
Open the KARR Security app.
Log in and select the correct vehicle.
Tap the Settings button in the lower-right corner.
Scroll down and tap Check for Updates.
Follow the instructions shown in the app.
Wait for confirmation that the firmware is current.
KARR says no additional action is necessary after the app confirms that the latest firmware is installed.
You can still check and update a device that remained in the vehicle after you declined the service.
Follow these steps:

Download the official KARR Security app.Sit in the driver's seat near the device.Open the app.Tap the Customer Service: 800-395-5277 link.Follow the app's instructions to check the VIN.Complete the firmware update when prompted.Confirm that the app reports the latest firmware.
Download the official KARR Security app.
Sit in the driver's seat near the device.
Open the app.
Tap the Customer Service: 800-395-5277 link.
Follow the app's instructions to check the VIN.
Complete the firmware update when prompted.
Confirm that the app reports the latest firmware.
Call KARR support when the app cannot find the vehicle or complete the update.
WAYMO RECALLS ROBOTAXIS OVER CONSTRUCTION-ZONE RISK

Drivers can check for a KARR or SWDS device by inspecting the driver-side window, dashboard area and vehicle sales paperwork. (David Baillot/University of California San Diego/Jacobs School of Engineering)
Should you remove the KARR device?

You can ask to have the system deactivated or removed. However, I would not turn this into a weekend do-it-yourself project. Researchers warn that removal may require opening the dashboard, cutting wires and restoring connections involving the ignition system or vehicle computers. Disconnecting the wrong wire could stop the car from starting. It might also affect the factory alarm, remote start or another electrical feature. Southwest Dealer Services says an owner can request removal, transfer or deactivation by calling 800-395-5277 and confirming the account information.

Ask the original dealership or a qualified automotive electrical technician to handle the work. Before approving removal, ask the technician how the factory wiring will be restored. Afterward, request written confirmation that the module was removed and the vehicle's original security functions still work.
We reached out to KARR Security, and a representative from the company provided CyberGuy with the following statement:

"KARR Security maintains rigorous standards to help protect customers’ vehicles. Researchers at UC San Diego identified a vulnerability affecting BLE-based auto theft devices, including a small percentage of KARR devices with certain Bluetooth-related components. The vulnerability described in the research is highly complex and presents a low risk to customers under real-world conditions. Nevertheless, we responded promptly and developed a firmware update to address the issue. We launched this app/firmware update on July 20, 2026. Active customers may apply the update directly from their phone after securely logging in to the KARR Security app. Vehicle owners of non-active systems can still update via the app using their VIN (last 8 digits) as a validation step. Consumers can find detailed instructions and tutorials for assistance with this firmware on the Customer FAQ section of our website at www.KARRSecurity.com."
KARR Security added, "To our knowledge, we have not seen this vulnerability used in the real world to break into or steal a vehicle."
What will not fix the KARR Bluetooth flaw

Turning off Bluetooth on your phone will not disable the Bluetooth radio inside the KARR module. Deleting the app will not remove the device. Removing the vehicle from your phone's normal Bluetooth menu will not patch it either.

The KARR module communicates separately from the Cadillac, Hyundai or other factory infotainment system. A Faraday pouch also will not fix this particular problem. Faraday pouches can help block relay attacks involving a key fob. They cannot update or disable hardware installed beneath the dashboard. You need to update the KARR device itself or have a professional remove it.
Tips to protect your vehicle from being stolen
Car thieves use different methods, so protecting your vehicle requires more than one piece of technology.

When your vehicle has a KARR or SWDS device, install the firmware update as soon as possible. This directly addresses the Bluetooth flaw identified by the researchers. A steering wheel lock or tracker can add protection, but neither one repairs vulnerable software.

Signal jammers can sometimes block the command sent by a key fob. After pressing the lock button, listen for the normal confirmation sound. Look for the lights and pull a door handle before walking away. Also, close every window and take the keys with you. NHTSA recommends checking the doors whenever you leave a parked vehicle.

A steering wheel lock creates an obvious barrier inside the car. It will not stop every determined thief. However, it adds time and makes the vehicle harder to steer. NHTSA includes steering wheel locks among visible devices that can discourage vehicle theft. You can find more ideas in my CyberGuy guide on how to help prevent your car from getting stolen.

Store key fobs away from exterior doors, windows and attached garages. A tested signal-blocking pouch can help reduce the risk of a relay attack. In that type of theft, criminals extend the signal from a key inside the house to a vehicle outside. Test the pouch regularly. Put the key inside, close the pouch and stand next to the car. The doors should remain locked when you touch the handle. Remember that a key-fob pouch protects against a different attack. It will not patch a KARR module.

A hidden GPS tracker or Bluetooth tracker may help locate a stolen vehicle. However, do not confront anyone or attempt to recover the car yourself. Give tracking information to law enforcement. An Apple AirTag can provide a backup location signal, although Apple's anti-stalking alerts may eventually warn a thief that an unknown AirTag is traveling with the vehicle. Read my CyberGuy guide on using an AirTag in a vehicle and understanding its limits.

Use a locked garage when one is available. Otherwise, park in a visible area with lighting, foot traffic or a security camera. Avoid isolated corners where someone can work around the vehicle without attracting attention. NHTSA also recommends parking in well-lit areas whenever possible.

A thief may break into a car without planning to steal the entire vehicle. Take phones, laptops, wallets and bags with you. Do not leave a spare key or garage remote inside the car. NHTSA warns that thieves commonly target electronics and other items they can quickly resell.
Kurt's key takeaways

Nancy's question highlights the biggest problem with this vulnerability. Many drivers have no idea that a KARR or SWDS device may be hiding in their vehicle. You will not find a KARR code inside your vehicle's settings. Look for a sticker on the driver-side window and a small aftermarket button below the dashboard. Then check your paperwork and ask the selling dealer to search your VIN. The flaw can unlock a vulnerable vehicle and interfere with its security features from nearby. It cannot start the engine by itself or shut down a moving car. Still, unlocking the doors may give a thief the access needed to try another method. Fortunately, KARR has released a firmware update. Install it through the official KARR Security app. When you no longer want the system, arrange professional removal rather than pulling wires yourself.
Should dealerships have to tell you about every connected device installed in your car, even when you decline to purchase the service? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Mom of slain Citadel cadet says son was 'such a light' as expert flags cellphones as potential motive break
summary: Dustin Rose's cellphone may reveal why he and Samson Campbell were killed in DeLand, Florida, as a former homicide detective explains the forensic audit.
story: Patrick McGeehan, a former homicide detective, told Fox News Digital that because the Citadel cadet and his best friend still had their phones, a robbery seems unlikely — and a forensic audit could reveal a motive.

The mother of a Citadel cadet killed alongside his best friend remembered her son as "such a light," while a former detective said the two victims' cellphones may hold the answer to why they were slain.
The DeLand Police Department in Florida said Dustin Rose, 19, and Samson Campbell, 18, were found dead at around 10:40 p.m. on July 29.
Officials announced on Tuesday that an arrest warrant was obtained for a 17-year-old male, who was arrested on Wednesday by the U.S. Marshals Service.
During a Wednesday news conference, authorities said the three people "knew each other in some capacity," and said the teenager who was arrested has a "pretty good criminal history."
TEEN ARRESTED ON MURDER CHARGES AFTER CITADEL CADET AND CHILDHOOD FRIEND FOUND SHOT DEAD
Dustin Rose, 19, a Citadel cadet, was pursuing his childhood dream of serving in the military when he was killed. (GoFundMe)

Rose attended The Citadel Military College of South Carolina and was home on break at the time. In a message to the campus community shared with Fox News Digital, The Citadel President Gen. Frank McKenzie described Rose as a "team leader and was a valued friend and classmate."
In addition, Rose was also a member of the South Carolina National Guard, a spokeswoman confirmed with Fox News Digital.
Rachel Rose, Dustin's mother, said he was "such a light in our family."
"When they took him they took the very best part of me. We are devastated," she told Fox News Digital.
CITADEL CADET, CHILDHOOD FRIEND GUNNED DOWN IN VACANT FLORIDA LOT AS POLICE LAUNCH MANHUNT
Childhood friends Dustin Rose, left, and Samson Campbell, right, were fatally shot in a vacant Florida lot. (DeLand Police Department)

Patrick McGeehan, a criminal defense attorney and former homicide detective, told Fox News Digital that since their phones weren't stolen, investigators could use them as they try to piece together a potential motive.

"And they still have the phone, the one kid still had the phone, which leads me to believe that's not a robbery. It may be something else, because who's going to leave a thousand dollar smart phone if they're doing robbery? That's something else that jumped out at me," McGeehan said. "They will go through their phones. They will do a forensic audit of their phones, that is something that agencies in the area are capable of doing."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
"The information they can gather from the phone is fairly extensive," he added.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Police released a screenshot of surveillance video showing the two walking together on Tuesday evening. It's not yet known if the two were targeted.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
One of the victims' mothers may have been among the family members who found the two dead after they went unreachable by phone, police previously said.
SEND US A TIP

Campbell, a DeLand native, had been staying with his aunt, Karen Chobin, in the Chicago area. Chobin said he was in town to grieve the recent death of the family's 8-year-old dog and was staying with Rose's grandparents.
GOT A TIP?
Rose was in DeLand to help Campbell spread his dog's ashes, Chobin said.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Surveillance video shows Dustin Rose and Samson Campbell walking together on Tuesday evening, the day before they were found dead. (DeLand Police Department)
"It was a traumatic loss. It wasn't a passing of old age. It was awful. And then for this to be what he's welcomed with when he goes down there to mourn his loss is devastating," Chobin said.
Rose's aunt, Jaimie Scarola, told FOX 35 his life was taken too soon.

"He was willing to go to the front line and fight for our freedom, including the freedom of the one who took him from us," Scarola said. "You took him away from not only his family, but you robbed an entire country of a future soldier who didn't get to answer that call."

title: Eyewitness describes suspicious encounter that helped launch Washington wildfire arson probe
summary: A Washington grandfather says he spotted a stranger bent over near railroad tracks minutes before smoke erupted and the Old Trails Fire ignited.
story: A Spokane arson suspect making his first court appearance in connection with the fires. Local CEO Brandon Schmidt joins to recount his evacuation efforts and describe the devastating impact of the fires on the community.

A Washington grandfather said a stranger lingering near a dead-end road where almost nobody goes immediately caught his attention – moments before smoke began rising from the same stretch of railroad tracks and a devastating wildfire erupted.
Paul Child was driving his grandson to pick up a friend Saturday when he noticed a bald man standing near the railroad tracks along West Euclid Road and staring into the tree line.
"I really didn’t think anything of it at that point," Child told Fox News Digital.
SPENCER PRATT REACTS TO SPOKANE DEVASTATION WITH BLUNT WILDFIRE WARNING AND MESSAGE OF FAITH
About 10 minutes later, Child drove back along the same road and noticed the man was still there.
Aaron F. Farinacci was arrested on suspicion of first-degree arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire in eastern Washington. (Arizona Department of Corrections)

"This time he was kind of bent over and looked like he was doing something in the brush or the bushes and the grass and the trees," Child said. "When he saw us, then he kind of stood up and was acting kind of nervous."
Even Child’s grandson sensed something was off.
"My grandson said, ‘What’s he doing?’" Child said.
The family returned to their home and minutes later, Child’s daughter, Ana Dillon, glanced toward the same stretch of railroad tracks.
"I just happened to look up and saw a huge cloud of white smoke, then black smoke," Dillon told Fox News Digital.
Child immediately connected the smoke to the stranger he had seen lingering near the tree line.
Aaron Farinacci, 37, was charged with first-degree arson. (Spokane County Sheriff’s Office)
"The first thing I thought was, ‘That SOB started the fire,’" Child alleged.
MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE

Child called 911 and tried to reach the only other homeowner on the dead-end stretch of road. The neighbor was not home, but Child reached him by phone and warned that a wildfire was moving toward the property, where workers were inside a shop behind the house.
"We drove down there and notified that person and told him maybe he should leave," Child said.
By then, firefighters had begun to arrive as flames spread across the dry grasslands and the family hurried to evacuate.

Heavy smoke blankets the Spokane area as firefighters battle several fast-moving wildfires that have forced thousands of evacuations and prompted a massive emergency response. (Spokane Valley Fire Department)
"The fire was coming toward us, so we packed up everything, everyone and animals," Dillon said.
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

Child said the family fled their nearly 17-acre property with five dogs and two cats, later flagging down an Airway Heights police officer and describing the man he had seen as a bald white male wearing a green T-shirt and backpack, court records show.
He also told officers where the man had been standing before smoke began rising from the area. Spokane County sheriff’s deputies soon detained a man matching the description.

Child, his grandson and the grandson’s friend then traveled with an Airway Heights police officer to where deputies were holding the suspect. Sitting inside Child’s pickup about 50 yards away, the three watched as deputies removed the man from a patrol vehicle and had him face them.
Chimneys are the only structures remaining in a residential neighborhood after a wildfire hit the northern part of Spokane, Washington, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. (AP Photo / Lindsey Wasson)
"The only thing I could really identify on him was his build and what he was wearing," Child said. "There was no question in any of our minds that was the individual we saw."
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT DISPLAYED 'INCEL ENERGY,' MADE WOMAN UNCOMFORTABLE DURING UBER RIDE: PASSENGER

Authorities later arrested Aaron F. Farinacci on suspicion of first-degree arson, accusing him of intentionally setting the Old Trails Fire, the largest of three wildfires that destroyed hundreds of buildings and forced about 67,000 people to evacuate.
Child said the family did not learn until the following day that deputies had initially released Farinacci before arresting him after investigators developed additional evidence.

Court records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Farinacci was previously charged with first-degree murder after fatally shooting his father during an argument in Arizona in 2010. He later pleaded guilty to reduced charges of manslaughter and aggravated assault, served about eight years in prison and was released in 2020.
Learning about Farinacci’s criminal history turned the family’s initial relief into concern, Child said.
"He knew where I lived," Child said. "Then to come to find out what his history was, it’s kind of like ... this dude could have come back down here."
Firefighters respond to a wildfire near Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue / FOX Weather)

Child said the man initially caught his attention because strangers rarely venture onto the family’s road. The county permanently closed the dead-end stretch several years ago, leaving only two homes beyond the barricade.

"There hasn’t been a lot of trespassing now," Child said. "If we see somebody down there, a lot of times we take it upon ourselves to pull up and say, ‘Are you OK?’ ... Nine times out of 10, they’re gone after that."
Dillon said anyone lingering near the tracks would immediately stand out to the family.

"There’s only two houses on this street," she said. "If anyone is on this street, we most always call Crime Check. No one should be on this road. It’s a closed road. Anyone standing and kneeling down by the train tracks that’s not a city worker is a red flag."

While Child’s observations helped point investigators toward a suspect, retired Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives executive Scott Sweetow said eyewitness accounts are only the beginning of a wildfire arson investigation.

Allen Sather stands in front of his 1968 Chevrolet C20 at the duplex he rented on West Indian Trail Road that burned in a wildfire in Spokane, Washington, Sunday, Aug. 2, 2026. (AP Photo / Young Kwak)

Fire investigators must first determine where a blaze started before they can establish how it ignited, Sweetow told Fox News Digital. That requires them to work backward from the aftermath, examine how the terrain and vegetation burned and eliminate plausible accidental causes.

"Arson fire in general is very hard to investigate," Sweetow said. "It requires a very meticulous focused effort that is not present in a lot of other investigations. And what complicates it is the fact that the evidence that you have to examine is often badly damaged by fire."

Investigators can reconstruct a fire’s earliest moments using witness accounts, video, cellphone data, first-responder observations and physical evidence. They also examine potential causes such as lightning, power infrastructure, trains, discarded smoking materials or other ignition sources.
That process can allow investigators to determine that a person started a fire even when no single item definitively establishes how it began, Sweetow said.

Sweetow cautioned against placing too much weight on any single piece of evidence, including investigators’ claim that Farinacci was carrying waterproof matches and a butane lighter when deputies first contacted him.

He said windproof and waterproof matches are more specialized than ordinary paper or wooden matches and are designed to remain lit in conditions that could extinguish a conventional match. Investigators would likely look for remnants of the same type of match near the fire’s point of origin, he said.

title: Trump's decade of assassination threats runs from Butler shooting to latest golf club breach
summary: From a 2016 rally gun grab to the 2026 White House Correspondents' Association Dinner attack, a timeline of assassination attempts and plots targeting Trump.

President Donald Trump’s decade in national politics has been continuously haunted by gunshots, armed stalkers and thwarted plots.
Two years after surviving a sniper's bullet in Butler, Pennsylvania, the president continues to navigate an unprecedented series of assassination attempts.

From his early campaign trail to the most recent security breach at Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes, the president has been threatened by a steady stream of danger throughout his second term.

Republican presidential candidate, former U.S. President Donald Trump is whisked away by the Secret Service after shots rang out at a campaign rally at Butler Farm Show Inc. on July 13, 2024, in Butler, Pennsylvania. (Jeff Swensen/Getty Images)

Ferrier also sent ricin letters to eight law enforcement officials in Texas and was arrested at the U.S.-Canada border with a loaded gun and hundreds of rounds of ammunition.

title: Florida man accused of cutting off diver's air supply in fight over coveted lobster diving spot
summary: A dispute over a lobster diving spot during Florida's lobster mini season allegedly turned deadly when a man shut off a diver's surface supplied air.
story: A man wanted on a felony warrant spent about 90 minutes in the Pacific Ocean off Will Rogers State Beach before Los Angeles County lifeguards surrounded him and helped take him into custody. (Credit: FOX 11 Los Angeles)

A battle over a lobster diving spot off the Florida coast allegedly escalated into an underwater nightmare after a man was accused of shutting off another diver's air supply, a confrontation that landed him behind bars on an attempted murder charge.

Michael Joseph Simpson, 51, surrendered Tuesday to the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center in Miami-Dade County, where he was booked Tuesday evening on an attempted murder charge, according to Miami-Dade jail records. His bond was set at $10,000.
According to Local 10 News, the incident occurred shortly after 7 a.m. on July 29 about a half-mile east of Fisher Island during Florida's annual lobster mini season.
Citing the arrest affidavit, Law&Crime reported that Simpson allegedly approached another boat at a high rate of speed and circled the vessel several times before anchoring about 10 feet away.
FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED FOR DUI AFTER TROOPERS ALLEGEDLY FIND 34 OPEN ALCOHOL CONTAINERS IN VEHICLE
Michael Joseph Simpson's booking photo after his arrest on an attempted murder charge in Miami-Dade County, Fla. (Miami-Dade County Corrections and Rehabilitation)
Investigators say the confrontation began after Simpson claimed the group was diving in "his spot" and warned that a larger boat was on its way before it arrived and anchored nearby.

Authorities allege Simpson then threatened to turn off the surface-supplied air system providing oxygen to an 18-year-old diver searching for lobsters. Investigators say Simpson jumped into the water and intentionally shut off the unit.
As the confrontation unfolded, witnesses yelled, "We have a diver down there you a--hole!" according to the arrest affidavit cited by Law&Crime.
The diver's boat owner jumped into the water and pulled him to the surface. The diver was gasping for air and appeared disoriented but was not injured, Local 10 reported.

title: American Airlines flight attendant's alleged killers tied to gang accused of preying on tourists: officials
summary: Two suspects captured in Peru months after allegedly drugging and killing American Airlines flight attendant Eric Fernando Gutierrez Molina in Medellín.
story: FBI Special Agent in Charge Jason Hudson details the U.S. extradition of alleged Tren de Aragua leader Jose Enrique Martinez Flores during a news conference, Friday May 15, 2026.

Two men accused of drugging and killing an American Airlines flight attendant during a layover in Colombia have been arrested months after the slaying, authorities said, with the suspects allegedly tied to a gang known to prey on tourists.

Andrés Felipe Peña Corrales, 23, and William Olave Gamboa, 31, were captured in Peru in connection with the March killing of Eric Fernando Gutierrez Molina, 32, a Dallas-based flight attendant whose disappearance in Medellín sparked an international search.

Peña Corrales has since been transferred to Colombia to face charges, while Olave Gamboa remains in Peruvian custody awaiting extradition proceedings. Both men face charges including aggravated homicide and aggravated robbery in Colombia, according to authorities.
AMERICANS WARNED POPULAR TRAVEL ROUTES THIS SUMMER COULD CARRY CRIME AND KIDNAPPING RISKS
Two suspects arrested in Peru are seen in police custody after authorities accused them in the killing of American Airlines flight attendant Eric Fernando Gutierrez Molina. (U.S. Embassy Bogota)

A third suspect, María del Carmen González, 24, was arrested separately in Montería, Colombia. Investigators allege she was not directly involved in Gutierrez Molina’s killing but participated in withdrawing and moving money stolen from foreign victims as part of the group’s operation.

Colombian police identified all three suspects as alleged members of Los Goteros, a criminal organization accused of targeting foreign tourists by contacting them through dating apps, gaining their trust, drugging them and stealing money, jewelry and other valuables.
According to reporting by El Colombiano, investigators believe Gutierrez Molina was contacted through a dating app before meeting several people at a nightclub in Medellín’s El Poblado neighborhood.
The group later went to a hotel, where Gutierrez Molina and his coworker were allegedly drugged before their belongings were stolen and their financial accounts were accessed, the outlet reported.

The outlet also reported that scopolamine, sometimes called "Devil’s Breath" or "Dragon’s Breath," may have been used to incapacitate the victims, though authorities have not publicly confirmed toxicology findings in the case.
Gutierrez Molina was reportedly strangled, while his coworker survived.
DATING-APP CHARMER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER HISTORY OF DOMESTIC ARRESTS INVOLVING WOMEN HE MET ONLINE
Investigators allege the group accessed Gutierrez Molina’s bank accounts, stole other valuables and abandoned his body near Jericó, southwest of Medellín, where it was found five days later.
The arrests capped a months-long international investigation involving U.S. Homeland Security Investigations, Colombian prosecutors and Peruvian authorities.

"This successful outcome reflects the strong commitment of the United States, Colombia and Peru to work together to investigate and bring to justice a group of criminals in Colombia dedicated to the robbery and theft of U.S. citizens and ensure the safety of international travelers in the region," the U.S. Embassy in Colombia said in a joint statement.
The embassy also recognized the Mayor’s Office of Medellín, Colombia’s National Police and Peru’s National Police for their roles in the investigation.
EXCLUSIVE: ALLEGED $32M COVID-19 FRAUD FUGITIVE CAPTURED IN JAMAICA AND RETURNED TO US, FBI SAYS

Authorities say American Airlines flight attendant Eric Fernando Gutierrez Molina was drugged, robbed and killed after an overnight layover in Medellín, Colombia, in March 2026. (Edinson Arroyo/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Gutierrez Molina disappeared in March while on an overnight layover in Medellín before he was scheduled to continue to Miami.

Friends told local media at the time that he shared his location from an Airbnb near José María Córdova International Airport before communication suddenly stopped, prompting coworkers and family members to report him missing.
Days later, Medellín Mayor Federico Gutiérrez announced that authorities had recovered a body near Jericó. The remains were later identified as Gutierrez Molina.

Eric Fernando Gutierrez Molina, a 32-year-old flight attendant from Dallas, was reported missing in Colombia after he arrived on Saturday, March 21, according to reports. (CDColExt/X)
"We are heartbroken by the tragic passing of our colleague," American Airlines said in a statement previously provided to Fox News Digital.
"Our thoughts and support are with his family, loved ones and colleagues during this difficult time, and we are doing all we can to assist Colombian law enforcement in its investigation."
Authorities said investigators are working to determine whether additional foreign tourists were victimized by Los Goteros using the same alleged scheme.

story: Alex Murdaugh returns to court for a retrial status hearing, following his overturned double murder conviction. Attorneys analyze the implications for both the Murdaugh case, including calls for new DNA evidence review and the Supreme Court's impact on state election procedures.
